texts.Chapter 6 opens with a quick review of n: Chapter 6 opens with a quick review of nouns, because the adjective endings you are about to learn borrow them. A noun sentence (A は B です) can be present or past, and positive or negative, which gives four forms. The book shows them with しゃいん (employee): です, では ありません or じゃ ありません, でした, and では ありません でした or じゃ ありません でした。
texts.To change a noun sentence to the past, o: To change a noun sentence to the past, only the end changes. です becomes でした, and じゃ ありません becomes じゃ ありません でした (just add でした). じゃ is the short form of では and both mean the same, so every じゃ ありません can also be では ありません. The book prints both in its tables and uses じゃ ありません in its drills, so this chapter does too.
texts.The past tense says that something was t: The past tense says that something was true earlier: かようび は しけん でした means Tuesday was the exam. Keep this pattern in mind, because な-adjectives are conjugated in exactly the same way (lesson 6.7).
texts.6.2 Two types of adjectives: i and na (b: 6.2 Two types of adjectives: い and な (ぶんけい 6.1)
texts.The first kind is the i-adjective (writt: The first kind is the い-adjective (written い-adjective). It ends in the sound い: たかい (expensive), おおきい (big), たのしい (enjoyable). That last い is the part that changes when you make the word negative or past, as you will see in lesson 6.6.
texts.The second kind is the na-adjective (wri: The second kind is the な-adjective (written な-adjective). It ends in other sounds, and it needs な only when it sits directly in front of a noun: きれいな へや (a clean room), いろいろな もんだい (various problems). The book's word lists show this by writing (な) after the word, for example かんたん(な). Before です the な is dropped: へやは きれいです means the room is clean.
texts.Here is the trap. Kirei (clean, beautifu: Here is the trap. きれい (clean, beautiful) and ゆうめい (famous) end in い, but they are な-adjectives. Sound alone cannot tell you the type, so learn the type together with each new word and look for the (な) mark. It matters because い-adjectives change their own ending (たかい, たかくない, たかかった), while な-adjectives stay the same and only です changes (きれいです, きれいでした).
texts.a kind teacher (i-adjective, no change b: a kind teacher (い-adjective, no change before a noun)
texts.a famous teacher (na-adjective, na befor: a famous teacher (な-adjective, な before a noun)
texts.The teacher is famous. (no na before des: The teacher is famous. (no な before です)

texts.The book teaches adjectives in 21 pairs: The book teaches adjectives in 21 pairs of opposites. Learn each pair together, because if you remember one half, the other half comes almost for free. Each row shows both words and their types, where い means い-adjective and な means な-adjective.
texts.Most pairs are i + i. The mixed pairs ar: Most pairs are い + い. The mixed pairs are かんたん(な) with むずかしい, きれい(な) with きたない and ひま(な) with いそがしい. The pairs where both words are な-adjectives are しずか(な) with にぎやか(な), and べんり(な) with ふべん(な).
texts.Three words show up in more than one pai: Three words show up in more than one pair. たかい means expensive (opposite やすい) and also high or tall (opposite ひくい). あつい is the busiest word: it means hot to the touch (opposite つめたい), hot weather (opposite さむい) and thick (opposite うすい). Only the situation and the opposite tell you which meaning is meant. Finally, いい and よい both mean good. They are the same word, but よい takes over when you conjugate, which lesson 6.6 explains.
texts.The main job of an adjective is to descr: The main job of an adjective is to describe a noun, and it goes right in front of the noun. With an い-adjective nothing changes: やさしい せんせい (a kind teacher), たかい じてんしゃ (an expensive bicycle). With a な-adjective you add な between the adjective and the noun: きれいな へや (a clean room), かんたんな しけん (an easy exam). The book calls this Adjective + Noun / Noun Phrase, which tells you that the thing being described can also be a longer phrase, like たかい たてもの (a tall building).
texts.Compare two ways of using the same adjec: Compare two ways of using the same adjective. へや は きれいです says the room is clean. The adjective ends the sentence, so there is no な. きれい な へや です says it is a clean room. The adjective sits in front of a noun, so な is needed. いろいろ(な) works the same way and always shows up as いろいろな before a noun: いろいろな もんだい (various problems).
texts.You can put the whole phrase anywhere a: You can put the whole phrase anywhere a noun fits, for example before です or before が あります: いえの ちかくに おおきい こうえんが あります.
texts.6.5 Adjective + adjective: kute and de (: 6.5 Adjective + adjective: くて and で (ぶんけい 6.3)
texts.With an i-adjective, drop the final i an: With an い-adjective, drop the final い and add くて: あたらしい becomes あたらしくて, so あたらしくて たかい means new and expensive. With a な-adjective, drop the な and add で: にぎやか(な) becomes にぎやか で, so にぎやかで りっぱな means lively and splendid. The same chains work in front of a noun, as in あつくて おもい ほん (a thick, heavy book). When the last adjective is a な-adjective in front of a noun, it keeps its な: きれい で しずか な ところ (a clean, quiet place).
texts.Only the last adjective carries desu and: Only the last adjective carries です and the tense. Say このへやは あかるくて ひろいです for This room is bright and wide, and put only the last word in the past: あかるくて ひろかった です。 いい (good) uses its other form here: よくて やすい means good and cheap.
texts.In practice, join qualities that go toge: In practice, join qualities that go together in mood, such as あかるくて ひろい (bright and wide) or むずかしくて つまらない (difficult and boring). Joining a good point with a bad point needs a different word, which this chapter does not cover.
texts.6.6 I-adjectives: present, past and nega: 6.6 い-adjectives: present, past and negative (adjective conjugation)
texts.With i-adjectives, the adjective itself: With い-adjectives, the adjective itself changes for negative and past, and です stays as the polite ending. Take the final い off and add くない for the negative, かった for the past, and くなかった for the past negative. So たかい (expensive) gives たかくない (not expensive), たかかった (was expensive) and たかくなかった (was not expensive).
texts.The book writes desu in brackets in its: The book writes です in brackets in its tables, because it can be dropped in casual speech. This whole book uses the polite style, so keep です: たかかったです. Do not change です to でした after an い-adjective. たかい でした is wrong, and たかかったです is right.
texts.Ii (good) is the only irregular adjectiv: いい (good) is the only irregular adjective. It cannot be conjugated, so its other form よい takes over: よくない (not good), よかった (was good) and よくなかった (was not good). Never say いいくない or いいかった. Also watch つまらない (boring). It ends in ない, but it is a normal い-adjective, so its negative is つまらなくない (not boring), and its past is つまらなかった.
texts.6.7 Na-adjectives: present, past and neg: 6.7 な-adjectives: present, past and negative (adjective conjugation)
texts.A na-adjective does not change at all. I: A な-adjective does not change at all. It is conjugated like a noun, so only the ending after it changes: きれいです (is clean), きれい じゃ ありません (is not clean), きれいでした (was clean) and きれい じゃ ありません でした (was not clean). You can swap じゃ for では in the negative forms, as the book does in its ひま examples.
texts.The na never appears in these four forms: The な never appears in these four forms, because な is only needed in front of a noun. Say きれいです, not きれい な です. This also explains why きれい, which ends in い, is not conjugated like an い-adjective. Never say きれくない. The negative of きれい is きれい じゃ ありません.
texts.Compare the two types side by side. An i: Compare the two types side by side. An い-adjective changes its own ending, as in たかい, たかくない, たかかった, たかくなかった. A な-adjective stays put, and the endings です, じゃ ありません, でした and じゃ ありません でした do the work.
texts.6.8 How is it? Dou desu ka and donna A d: 6.8 How is it? どう です か and どんな A です か (ぶんけい 6.4)
Two question words ask about adjectives. どう means how, and it asks for a description: A は どう です か means How is A? どんな plus a noun means what kind of, and it asks what sort of thing or person something is: どんな A です か means What kind of A is it? Both questions are always answered with adjectives.
texts.Use dou at the end of the sentence, as i: Use どう at the end of the sentence, as in にほんごの クラスは どうですか, and answer with A は adjective です. Use どんな directly in front of a noun, as in たなかさんは どんな ひとですか, and answer with an adjective plus the same noun: やさしい ひとです. For a past question, change です to でした: きのうの りょうりは どうでしたか (How was the dish yesterday?). The answer then uses a past adjective, for example おいしかったです.
texts.6.9 Very: taihen and totemo (bunkei 6.5): 6.9 Very: たいへん and とても (ぶんけい 6.5)
texts.Taihen and totemo both mean very. Put ei: たいへん and とても both mean very. Put either one directly in front of the adjective and leave everything else alone: やさしい です becomes たいへん やさしい です, and たかいです becomes とても たかいです. They also work in the past (とても あつかった です), and in front of a noun phrase (とても きれい な くに).
texts.The book treats the two words as the sam: The book treats the two words as the same. とても is the one you will hear most in everyday talk, and たいへん sounds a little more formal. Both go with positive adjectives only. To say not very, use あまり with a negative ending, which comes in the next lesson.
texts.6.10 A little and not very: chotto and a: 6.10 A little and not very: ちょっと and あまり (ぶんけい 6.6)
texts.Chotto means a little. Put it in front o: ちょっと means a little. Put it in front of an adjective, and the adjective keeps its normal form: ちょっと せまい です (it is a little small). ちょっと also makes a refusal sound soft. すみません, いま ちょっと いそがしい です is a polite way to say you cannot do something now.
texts.Amari means not very, and it must always: あまり means not very, and it must always be followed by a negative ending. Say あまり たかくないです (not very expensive) or あまり かんたん じゃ ありません (not very easy), and never あまり たかいです. It works in the past as well: あまり むずかしくなかった です (it was not very difficult).
texts.To pick the right adverb, remember this:: To pick the right adverb, remember this: とても, たいへん and ちょっと go with positive endings, and あまり goes only with negative endings.
texts.This last lesson is an extra that pulls: This last lesson is an extra that pulls the chapter together, because the exercises mix everything. A full adjective sentence follows the pattern A は (adverb) adjective です. The adverb is optional, and the last word of the sentence carries the tense.
texts.A yes or no question just adds ka, and y: A yes or no question just adds か, and you answer with はい or いいえ. In a no answer the adjective turns negative: いいえ、ひまじゃありません. You can also give the true answer after it, as in いいえ、あつくなかったです。 さむかったです (No, it was not hot. It was cold.).
texts.To describe where something is, build th: To describe where something is, build the description in front of the noun and finish with に あります or が あります: いえの ちかくに ひろくて しずかな こうえんが あります. When two adjectives describe one noun, the first one joins with くて or で, and the last one goes straight in front of the noun (with な if it needs it).
texts.Kirei and yuumei end in i but are na-adj: きれい and ゆうめい end in い but are な-adjectives
texts.kirei (clean, beautiful) and yuumei (fam: きれい (clean, beautiful) and ゆうめい (famous) look like い-adjectives, but they are な-adjectives.

texts.The negative is kirei ja arimasen, never: The negative is きれい じゃ ありません, never きれくない.
texts.Look for the (na) mark in the vocabulary: Look for the (な) mark in the vocabulary list whenever you learn a new adjective.

texts.The same goes for shizuka, benri, kantan: The same goes for しずか, べんり, かんたん, にぎやか, ひま, ふべん, りっぱ, いろいろ and ゆうめい。
texts.The adjective changes, not desu: takakat: The adjective changes, not です: たかかったです (was expensive), never たかい でした.
texts.Negative: takakunai desu. Past negative:: Negative: たかくないです. Past negative: たかくなかったです.
texts.The word ii is the exception. It uses yo: The word いい is the exception. It uses よい, so you get よくない, よかった and よくなかった。
texts.A na-adjective works like a noun: desu b: A な-adjective works like a noun: です becomes でした, and じゃ ありません gets でした added.
texts.Tsumaranai ends in nai but is not a nega: つまらない ends in ない but is not a negative
texts.tsumaranai (boring) is a normal i-adject: つまらない (boring) is a normal い-adjective that happens to end in ない.
texts.Its negative is tsumaranakunai (not bori: Its negative is つまらなくない (not boring), and its past is つまらなかった.
texts.The negative ending kunai is added to ot: The negative ending くない is added to other adjectives, such as たかくない.
texts.Ja arimasen and dewa arimasen: じゃ ありません and では ありません
Both mean the same, and both are polite. じゃ is the short form of では.
texts.The word dewa is written では, and the は i: The word では is written では, and the は is read は.
texts.Add deshita to either one for the past:: Add でした to either one for the past: じゃ ありません でした or では ありません でした。

texts.An i-adjective drops the final i and add: An い-adjective drops the final い and adds くて: あかるくて ひろい。
texts.A na-adjective adds de: kirei de yasashi: A な-adjective adds で: きれい で やさしい。
texts.The word ii becomes yokute: yokute yasui: The word いい becomes よくて: よくて やすい。
texts.Only the last adjective carries the tens: Only the last adjective carries the tense: あかるくて ひろかった です。

texts.kaigi wa nagai desu ka. (かいぎは ながいですか。): かいぎは ながいですか。
Add か to make it a question.
texts.kinou wa atsukatta desu ka. iie, samukat: きのうは あつかったですか。 いいえ、さむかったです。
texts.atsui and samui are the weather words fo: あつい and さむい are the weather words for hot and cold. いいえ、あつくなかったです。 さむかったです. is also fine.

texts.7.1 Verbs in the formal form (masu, mase: 7.1 Verbs in the formal form (ます, ません, ました, ません でした)
texts.This is the first chapter with verbs, wh: This is the first chapter with verbs, which are the action words: wake up, sleep, work, study. The book uses the formal (polite) form for now. It is built from a verb stem plus an ending. The stem is what is left when you take ます (ます) off: ね for ねます, おき for おきます and はじまり for はじまります.
texts.Four endings give you four forms. Masu i: Four endings give you four forms. ます is the present positive, ません is the present negative, ました is the past positive and ません でした is the past negative. The book shows the pattern with ねます: ねます (sleep), ねません (do not sleep), ねました (slept) and ねませんでした (did not sleep). Notice that the past negative is the only form with two words, ません plus でした, just like じゃ ありません でした in Chapter 6.
texts.Japanese has no separate future tense. T: Japanese has no separate future tense. The present form covers both now and later, so らいげつ おわります means it finishes next month. The time word in the sentence tells you which one is meant. Words such as べんきょう (study), しごと (work), ざんぎょう (overtime) and きゅうけい (break) become verbs when you add します, and only the します part changes: べんきょうしません, べんきょうしました, べんきょうしません でした。
texts.Umaremasu (be born) is in the word list,: うまれます (be born) is in the word list, but the workbook never uses it. Because being born has already happened, you will mostly meet it in the past: うまれました. The dictionary form of verbs, the one you look up in a dictionary, comes later in Chapter 9, so for now you only need the ます forms.
texts.work (shigoto plus shimasu): work (しごと plus します)
texts.7.2 Time expression + ni + verb (bunkei: 7.2 Time expression + に + verb (ぶんけい 7.1)
texts.The marker ni goes after a specific time: The marker に goes after a specific time and tells you when the action happens: at 5:30, on Saturday, in December. The pattern is time + に + verb, and it works with all four verb forms.
texts.Ni is used only with specific times: a c: に is used only with specific times: a clock time (ごじ はん に), a day of the week (どようび に), a month (じゅうにがつ に) or a date (とおか に). Time words that are not specific take no に. These are the relative words such as きのう, あした, あさって, ゆうべ, こんばん, まいにち, まいあさ, けさ, こんしゅう, せんしゅう, らいしゅう, らいげつ and せんせんしゅう. You say らいげつ おわります, never らいげつ に おわります.
texts.Here is a quick test. If the time word c: Here is a quick test. If the time word could be the answer to なんじ (what time), なんようび (what day of the week), なんがつ (what month) or なんにち (what day of the month), then it takes に. Words like きのう and まいにち do not answer any of those, so they take no に.
The rows below use the book's examples. The verb part of each sentence does not change when you add に. Pay attention to which rows have a に and which do not.
texts.7.3 Time expression + kara + verb (bunke: 7.3 Time expression + から + verb (ぶんけい 7.2)
texts.Kara means from, and it marks the time w: から means from, and it marks the time when something starts. You met から in Chapter 4 in sentences like くじ から です. Now it goes in front of a verb: さんじから きゅうけいします means take a break from 3 o'clock.
texts.Kara goes straight after the time word,: から goes straight after the time word, with no に added. You say さんじ から, not さんじ に から. It also works with relative words such as あした and らいげつ, so あしたから べんきょうします is study from tomorrow.
texts.Kara and made are a natural pair, becaus: から and まで are a natural pair, because together they give the start and the end of an action: くじから じゅうじまで きゅうけいします. The next lesson looks at まで.
texts.7.4 Time expression + made + verb (bunke: 7.4 Time expression + まで + verb (ぶんけい 7.3)
texts.Made means until, and it marks the time: まで means until, and it marks the time when something stops. Like から, it goes straight after the time word with no に: くじはんまで きゅうけいしました is took a break until 9:30.
texts.Made works best with verbs that go on fo: まで works best with verbs that go on for a while, such as やすみます (rest), しごとします (work), べんきょうします (study) and きゅうけいします (take a break). That is why you do not see it with a one-moment verb like おきます. It makes sense to rest until March, but it does not make much sense to wake up until March.
texts.You can combine the two markers to say f: You can combine the two markers to say from when until when, as in げつようびから きんようびまで しごとします (work from Monday until Friday). The same words から and まで worked with places in Chapter 5, so you are just reusing them with time.
texts.7.5 Time expression + goro + verb (bunke: 7.5 Time expression + ごろ + verb (ぶんけい 7.4)
texts.Goro means around, and it gives a rough: ごろ means around, and it gives a rough time. It goes right after the time word: しちじはんごろ おきます is wake up around 7:30. You first met ごろ in Chapter 4.
texts.Goro is for a point in time, such as 7:3: ごろ is for a point in time, such as 7:30, next week, lunchtime or August. It is not for a length of time. For an amount of time you use ぐらい from Chapter 5: ろくじかんぐらい ねます is sleep about 6 hours. A simple way to remember it is ごろ for the clock and ぐらい for the length.
texts.The book writes goro without ni after it: The book writes ごろ without に after it, so follow that for now: ろくじごろ おきます. If you are not sure which one to use, ask yourself whether the word names a moment (ごろ) or tells how long something lasts (ぐらい).
texts.7.6 Span of time + de + verb (bunkei 7.5: 7.6 Span of time + で + verb (ぶんけい 7.5)
texts.This pattern uses a length of time, not: This pattern uses a length of time, not a point on the clock. Span of time + で + verb says that the action will happen within that length of time: さんじゅっぷんで おわります is finish within 30 minutes, and いちじかんで はじまります is start within an hour. Think of で as showing how much time passes or is needed before the action.
texts.The spans come from Chapter 5: sanjuppun: The spans come from Chapter 5: さんじゅっぷん (30 minutes), いちじかん (1 hour), じゅうごふん (15 minutes) and いっかげつ (1 month). Do not mix them up with clock times. いちじ is one o'clock, but いちじかん is one hour.
texts.Add ato in front to say after: ato juugo: Add あと in front to say after: あと じゅうごふんで きゅうけいします is take a break after 15 minutes. The book marks あと with a star because it is extra. The sentence works without it, and あと just makes the meaning clearer.
texts.Be careful with ni. A length of time wit: Be careful with に. A length of time with で does not take に, so you say いちじかん で, never いちじかん に で. に after a length of time is used for something else, how often, which is lesson 7.12.
texts.7.7 I-adjective as an adverb (bunkei 7.6: 7.7 い-adjective as an adverb (ぶんけい 7.6)
texts.An adjective can describe how an action: An adjective can describe how an action is done. To use an い-adjective this way, drop the final い and add く, then put it right before the verb. はやい (early) becomes はやく, so はやく おきます is wake up early. おそい (late) becomes おそく, so おそく ねました is slept late.
texts.The word ii (good) does not change direc: The word いい (good) does not change directly. As in Chapter 6, it borrows its other form よい, so you get よく: よく ねました is slept well. はやい and おそい each have two meanings, early or fast and late or slow. In this chapter, with these verbs, they mean early and late.
texts.Do not use kute here. In Chapter 6 you a: Do not use くて here. In Chapter 6 you added くて to join two adjectives, as in あかるくて ひろい. Before a verb you want plain く, so はやく おきます is right and はやくて おきます is wrong.
Notice that only the adjective changes. The verb keeps its own form, so you can use the same はやく with おきます, おきました or おきません。
texts.well (from ii, which uses yoi): well (from いい, which uses よい)
7.8 な-adjective as an adverb (ぶんけい 7.7)
texts.A na-adjective can also describe an acti: A な-adjective can also describe an action, but it changes in a different way. Drop the な and add に, then put it in front of the verb. しずか な becomes しずかに, so しずかに きゅうけいします is take a break quietly. まじめ な becomes まじめに, so まじめに べんきょうしました is studied seriously.
texts.That is the na in the (na) mark of the w: That is the な in the (な) mark of the word lists: it is the part that is replaced. In front of a noun the な stays, as in しずか な がくせい (a quiet student). In front of a verb it becomes に, as in しずかに べんきょうします (study quietly).
texts.Kirei and kantan from Chapter 6 are na-a: きれい and かんたん from Chapter 6 are な-adjectives too, so they also take に: きれいに はたらきます and かんたんに おわりました. Remember that the sound of the word does not decide the type. きれい ends in い but still uses に, not く.
texts.A quick way to choose: i-adjectives take: A quick way to choose: い-adjectives take く and な-adjectives take に. Lesson 7.13 puts both side by side.
texts.in good health, well (from genki na): in good health, well (from げんき な)
texts.cleanly, nicely (from kirei na): cleanly, nicely (from きれい な)
texts.Tokidoki means sometimes. You add it to: ときどき means sometimes. You add it to a sentence to say that the action is done now and then. はちじ に おきます is wake up at 8 o'clock, and ときどき はちじに おきます is sometimes wake up at 8 o'clock.
texts.The book puts tokidoki at the start of t: The book puts ときどき at the start of the sentence, in front of the time and the other details. You do not change the verb or add any marker. In the third row, おそく まで means until late, which is おそく (late) plus まで (until).
texts.Tokidoki is one of three how-often words: ときどき is one of three how-often words in this chapter. The other two are いつも (always, next lesson) and ぜんぜん (never, lesson 7.11).
texts.Itsumo means always. Like tokidoki, it g: いつも means always. Like ときどき, it goes at the start of the sentence and does not change the verb: ろくじ に おきます is wake up at 6 o'clock, and いつも ろくじに おきます is always wake up at 6 o'clock.
texts.The sentence does not have to be positiv: The sentence does not have to be positive. いつも ざんぎょうしません means always do not work overtime, which comes out as never work overtime. Be careful, because ぜんぜん (next lesson) can give a very similar meaning. いつも with a negative says it is always not done, while ぜんぜん says it is not done at all.
texts.Kurisumasu wa yasumimasu in the third ro: クリスマス は やすみます in the third row uses は to mark Christmas as the topic, and it means take Christmas off. Christmas is not a time like 6 o'clock, so the sentence has no に.
texts.7.11 Zenzen + negative (bunkei 7.10): 7.11 ぜんぜん + negative (ぶんけい 7.10)
texts.Zenzen means never or not at all, and it: ぜんぜん means never or not at all, and it always needs a negative ending. ごじ はん に おきません is do not wake up at 5:30, and ごじはんに ぜんぜん おきません is never wake up at 5:30.
texts.Put zenzen right before the verb or the: Put ぜんぜん right before the verb or the adverb that goes with it. When the sentence has a time word, ぜんぜん comes after it: ごじはんに ぜんぜん おきません. When there is no time word, it can start the sentence: ぜんぜん おそく ねません.
texts.Zenzen works in the past too, with masen: ぜんぜん works in the past too, with ません でした: きのう ぜんぜん べんきょうしませんでした is did not study at all yesterday. You cannot use it with a positive verb, so ぜんぜん おきます is wrong.
texts.This works just like amari from Chapter: This works just like あまり from Chapter 6. Both need a negative ending, but they say different things. あまり means not very, a little bit true, while ぜんぜん means not at all, not true in any way.
texts.The exercises keep asking questions abou: The exercises keep asking questions about time, so here is a map of the question words. なんじ に asks at what time, and you answer with a clock time plus に: ろくじ に おきます. なんじ ごろ asks around what time, and you answer with ごろ: ろくじごろ おきます. いつ asks when, and it takes no に: にほんご の クラス は いつ はじまります か。
texts.Nanjikan asks for a length of time, how: なんじかん asks for a length of time, how many hours. You answer with a length such as ろくじかん or ななじかん, and ぐらい makes it about: なんじかん ぐらい べんきょうします か. Do not confuse it with なんじ, which is a clock time. A good test is that なんじ goes with に and ごろ, and なんじかん goes with ぐらい and で。
texts.To say how often, use a length of time p: To say how often, use a length of time plus に, then the number of times: いっしゅうかんに にかい やすみます is rest twice a week. Ask it with なんかい (how many times). You learned this pattern in Chapter 5, and the counts are いっかい (once), にかい (twice), さんかい (three times) and so on.
texts.Finally, donogurai from Chapter 5 asks h: Finally, どのぐらい from Chapter 5 asks how long something takes, and you answer with a length and かかります: フィリピン から にほん まで ひこうき で よじかん ぐらい かかります。
texts.This last lesson pulls the chapter toget: This last lesson pulls the chapter together, because the exercises mix everything. A sentence with a verb usually follows this order: the topic with は, the time (with に if it is a specific time), a how-often word or adverb, and the verb at the very end. For example, まいあさ ろくじごろ はやく おきます has a time word, a ごろ time, an adverb and then the verb.
texts.The verb always comes last, and it carri: The verb always comes last, and it carries the tense. Match the tense to the time word. きのう, ゆうべ, けさ, おととい, せんしゅう and せんげつ are in the past, so use ました or ません でした。 あした, あさって, こんばん, こんしゅう, らいしゅう and らいげつ are in the future, so use ます or ません。 まいにち, まいあさ and まいばん describe habits, so they use ます or ません とお。
texts.When an adjective describes the verb, an: When an adjective describes the verb, an い-adjective drops its い and takes く, and a な-adjective takes に: はやく おきます and まじめに べんきょうします. A な-adjective in front of a noun keeps な instead: まじめ な がくせい. So for a な-adjective, な goes before a noun and に goes before a verb.
texts.Finally, the negative words zenzen and a: Finally, the negative words ぜんぜん and あまり need a negative verb, while いつも and ときどき can go with positive or negative verbs. When you write an answer, check four things in order: the marker (に or none), the adverb ending (く or に), the how-often word, and the verb tense.
texts.A specific time takes ni: goji han ni, d: A specific time takes に: ごじ はん に, どようび に, じゅうにがつ に, とおか に。
texts.Relative time words take no ni: kinou, a: Relative time words take no に: きのう, あした, あさって, ゆうべ, こんばん, まいにち, まいあさ, けさ, こんしゅう, せんしゅう, らいしゅう and らいげつ。
texts.Quick test: if the word could answer nan: Quick test: if the word could answer なんじ, なんようび, なんがつ or なんにち, use に.
texts.The words kara, made and goro sit straig: The words から, まで and ごろ sit straight after the time, so you do not add に: さんじ から, くじ はん まで, ろくじ ごろ。
texts.goro is around a point in time: rokuji g: ごろ is around a point in time: ろくじ ごろ (around 6 o'clock), らいしゅう ごろ (around next week).
texts.gurai is about a length of time: rokujik: ぐらい is about a length of time: ろくじかん ぐらい (about 6 hours).
texts.Ask yourself whether the word names a mo: Ask yourself whether the word names a moment or tells how long. A moment takes ごろ and a length takes ぐらい.
texts.ji is a clock time: rokuji is 6 o'clock,: じ is a clock time: ろくじ is 6 o'clock, and なんじ asks what time.
texts.jikan is a length of time: rokujikan is: じかん is a length of time: ろくじかん is 6 hours, and なんじかん asks how many hours.
texts.rokuji ni nemasu means sleep at 6. rokuj: ろくじ に ねます means sleep at 6. ろくじかん ねます means sleep for 6 hours.
texts.A clock time takes ni. A length of time: A clock time takes に. A length of time takes no に, except in the how-often pattern: いっしゅうかん に にかい。
texts.Kara, made and de: から, まで and で
texts.kara is the start and made is the end: k: から is the start and まで is the end: くじ から じゅうじ まで。
texts.de after a length of time means within i: で after a length of time means within it: いちじかん で おわります。
texts.Do not use de with a clock time. juuji d: Do not use で with a clock time. じゅうじ で does not mean until 10 o'clock, because まで does that.
texts.Put ato in front for after: ato juugofun: Put あと in front for after: あと じゅうごふんで きゅうけいします.
texts.An i-adjective takes ku before a verb: h: An い-adjective takes く before a verb: はやく おきます.
texts.A na-adjective takes ni before a verb: s: A な-adjective takes に before a verb: しずかに べんきょうします。
texts.A na-adjective takes na before a noun: s: A な-adjective takes な before a noun: しずか な がくせい。
texts.kirei ends in i but it is a na-adjective: きれい ends in い but it is a な-adjective, so say きれいに, never きれく.
texts.Ku, not kute, before a verb: く, not くて, before a verb
texts.kute joins two adjectives, as in akaruku: くて joins two adjectives, as in あかるくて ひろい.
texts.Before a verb, use plain ku: hayaku okim: Before a verb, use plain く: はやく おきます. はやくて おきます is wrong.
texts.The same split works for na-adjectives:: The same split works for な-adjectives: で joins two adjectives, and に goes before a verb.
texts.Hayai and osoi have two meanings: はやい and おそい have two meanings
texts.hayai means early or fast, and osoi mean: はやい means early or fast, and おそい means late or slow.
texts.With okimasu, nemasu and hajimarimasu th: With おきます, ねます and はじまります they mean early and late.
The adverb forms are はやく and おそく。
texts.ii (good) uses yoi, so its adverb form i: いい (good) uses よい, so its adverb form is よく, as in よく ねました.
texts.Masen or masen deshita: ません or ません でした
texts.masen is present or future, and masen de: ません is present or future, and ません でした is past.
texts.The time word decides. kinou, yuube, kes: The time word decides. きのう, ゆうべ, けさ, おととい and せんしゅう are past.
texts.kinou zenzen benkyoushimasen is wrong. S: きのう ぜんぜん べんきょうしません is wrong. Say きのう ぜんぜん べんきょうしませんでした.
texts.ashita, konban, raishuu and raigetsu are: あした, こんばん, らいしゅう and らいげつ are future, so use ます or ません。
texts.Zenzen and amari: ぜんぜん and あまり
texts.zenzen means not at all: zenzen benkyous: ぜんぜん means not at all: ぜんぜん べんきょうしません is do not study at all.
texts.amari means not very: amari benkyoushima: あまり means not very: あまり べんきょうしません is do not study very much.
texts.amari is from Chapter 6. zenzen is the s: あまり is from Chapter 6. ぜんぜん is the stronger of the two.
texts.Itsumo, tokidoki and zenzen: いつも, ときどき and ぜんぜん
texts.itsumo is always, tokidoki is sometimes: いつも is always, ときどき is sometimes and ぜんぜん is never.
texts.All three go at the start of the sentenc: All three go at the start of the sentence or right before the verb: いつも ろくじに おきます.

texts.Hatarakimasu and shigotoshimasu: はたらきます and しごとします

texts.shigotoshimasu is just shigoto (work) pl: しごとします is just しごと (work) plus します.
texts.The same trick works with benkyou, zangy: The same trick works with べんきょう, ざんぎょう and きゅうけい。
texts.Only the shimasu part changes: benkyoush: Only the します part changes: べんきょうしません, べんきょうしました。
texts.Yasumimasu, nemasu and yasumi: やすみます, ねます and やすみ
texts.yasumimasu means rest or take a day off,: やすみます means rest or take a day off, and ねます means sleep.
texts.yasumi (a noun) is a holiday or a rest d: やすみ (a noun) is a holiday or a rest day, and ひるやすみ is a lunch break.
texts.kyuukeishimasu is a short break during t: きゅうけいします is a short break during the day.
texts.nemui (sleepy) shares its root with nema: ねむい (sleepy) shares its root with ねます (sleep).
texts.hajimarimasu (start) and hatarakimasu (w: はじまります (start) and はたらきます (work) both begin with は.
texts.okimasu (wake up) and owarimasu (finish): おきます (wake up) and おわります (finish) both begin with を.
texts.okimasu and nemasu are opposites, and so: おきます and ねます are opposites, and そ あれ はじまります and おわります。
texts.Nanji, nanjikan, nankai and itsu: なんじ, なんじかん, なんかい and いつ

texts.The sentence tells you which one: isshuu: The sentence tells you which one: いっしゅうかんに にかい やすみます is rest twice a week.

texts.Chapter 7 gave you verbs that stand on t: Chapter 7 gave you verbs that stand on their own, like おきます (wake up) and ねます (sleep). Chapter 8 adds verbs that do something to something else, such as eat bread, read a book or write an email. These are called transitive verbs, and the thing the verb acts on is called the object. In Japanese the verb always comes last, and a small marker after each word tells you the job of that word. The next lessons go through those markers one by one.
texts.All the verbs in this chapter are in the: All the verbs in this chapter are in the formal ます form from Chapter 7, so they have the same four endings: ます, ません, ました and ません でした. Take たべます (eat) as the model. たべません is do not eat, たべました is ate and たべませんでした is did not eat. The stem is what is left when you drop ます, so たべ, のみ and よみ are the stems of たべます, のみます and よみます. The present form also covers the future, so たべます can mean eat or will eat.
texts.The chapter has 13 verbs, and they are l: The chapter has 13 verbs, and they are listed below. The dictionary form, the one you look up in a dictionary, comes later in Chapter 9, so for now you only need the ます forms.
texts.Four of the verbs have more than one mea: Four of the verbs have more than one meaning. ききます is listen or ask, はなします is speak or talk, みます is watch, look or see, and おしえます is teach or tell. The markers around the verb tell you which meaning is meant. かけます is almost always used in the set phrase でんわを かけます, which means make a phone call.
texts.8.2 A wa object o transitive verb (bunke: 8.2 A は object を transitive verb (ぶんけい 8.1)
The basic pattern is A は object を verb. は marks the topic, who does the action. O marks the object, the thing the action is done to. The verb comes last and shows the tense and whether it is positive or negative. So アナさんは とけいを かいます is Ana will buy a watch. In kana the object marker is written を, but you say it just like the vowel お. A good habit is to ask what the action is done to, and then put を straight after that word.
texts.The topic can be left out when everyone: The topic can be left out when everyone knows who is doing the action. とけい を かいます on its own is fine, and it means I will buy a watch if you are the one talking. Remember that the present form also covers the future.
texts.The book adds a note about negative sent: The book adds a note about negative sentences. When the verb is negative, the object marker を can change into は to put the spotlight on that thing, for emphasis. ビール を のみます is I drink beer, and ワインは のみません says that wine is the thing I do not drink. は is natural when you are comparing two things. You can also keep を in a negative sentence, as in the book's own example しょうせつ を よみません, and that is fine too.
texts.8.3 Time expression ni, kara, made or go: 8.3 Time expression に, から, まで or ごろ + transitive verb (ぶんけい 8.2)
texts.The time words from Chapter 7 slot in be: The time words from Chapter 7 slot in before the object, so the pattern is time + object を + verb. The markers are the ones you already know: に (at), から (from), まで (until) and ごろ (around). まいあさ あさごはんを たべます is I eat breakfast every morning, and いとうせんせいは さんじから おしえます is Mr. Ito teaches from 3 o'clock.
texts.The book has a note here. Ni is only for: The book has a note here. に is only for a specific time, such as a clock time, a day of the week, a month or a date. It is not used with non-specific time words like まいあさ, まいばん, まいにち, まいしゅう, けさ and きのう. Look at the rows to see the difference: にちようびに あたらしい くつを かいました has に, while けさ ぎゅうにゅうを のみました does not. から, まで and ごろ sit straight after the time word and never take に.
texts.The time word also helps you choose the: The time word also helps you choose the tense. けさ (this morning) and きのう (yesterday) are already past, so the verb ends in ました.
texts.8.4 Place of action de (bunkei 8.3): 8.4 Place of action で (ぶんけい 8.3)
texts.De marks the place where an action happe: で marks the place where an action happens or will happen, in English at or in. The pattern is place + で + (object を) + verb. きっさてん で コーヒー を のみます is I drink coffee at the coffee shop. The question word is どこで, which means where.
Do not mix で up with に from Chapter 5. に goes with います and あります to say where a person or a thing is. で goes with an action verb like のみます, たべます or べんきょうします to say where something happens. Compare the last two rows: かいしゃで はたらきます is work at the company, and かいしゃに います is be at the company.
texts.8.5 Recipient of action ni (bunkei 8.4): 8.5 Recipient of action に (ぶんけい 8.4)
texts.Ni marks the person who receives the act: に marks the person who receives the action, in English to or for. The pattern is person + に + (object を) + verb. Ana さん に でんわを かけます is I will call Ana. The English word changes with the verb. You call to Ana, write to Mr. Tanaka and buy something for your brother, but Japanese uses the same に each time. English also drops the little word in ask the teacher, and Japanese still says せんせいに ききました.
texts.Notice what this does to kikimasu. With: Notice what this does to ききます. With を after a thing, as in おんがくを ききます, it means listen. With に after a person, as in せんせい に ききます, it means ask. The question words for a recipient are だれ に and the more polite どなた に.
texts.8.6 Companion to or to issho ni (bunkei: 8.6 Companion to or to いっしょに (ぶんけい 8.5)
texts.To marks the person who does the action: と marks the person who does the action together with you, in English with. The pattern is person + to + (object を) + verb. しゃちょう to はなしました is I spoke with the company president. You can add いっしょに to stress the word together, as in あねといっしょに えいがを みました. The question words are だれ to and the more polite どなた to.
texts.Ni or to? Ask yourself whether the other: に or と? Ask yourself whether the other person joins in. If they do the action with you, use to. If they only receive the action, use に. ともだち to おんがくを ききます is listen to music with a friend, but ともだちに でんわを かけます is call a friend. With はなします both can work: しゃちょうと はなしました is spoke with the president, and おかあさんに はなしました is spoke to my mother.
texts.The same word to also joins two nouns an: The same word to also joins two nouns and then it means and, as in pan to くだもの (bread and fruit). After a person and right before the verb it means with. The book's English for the Kim row says cellphone, but コーラ is cola, so I wrote cola.
texts.8.7 Method of action de (bunkei 8.6): 8.7 Method of action で (ぶんけい 8.6)
texts.De also marks the method, which means ho: で also marks the method, which means how you do the action. Language words belong here, so にほんごで レポートを かきました is I wrote the report in Japanese. The same goes for えいごで おしえます (teach in English) and かんこくご で はなしました (spoke in Korean).
texts.De also works with other ways of doing t: で also works with other ways of doing things, such as でんわ で (by phone) or テレビ で (on TV). The question words are どうやって, which means how, and なにで. Do not add anything to the noun before で, so you say えいご で, not えいご の で.
texts.8.8 Tool of action de (bunkei 8.7): 8.8 Tool of action で (ぶんけい 8.7)
texts.When de marks a tool, it is the thing yo: When で marks a tool, it is the thing you use to do the action, in English with or using. はし で ラーメンを たべます is I eat ramen with chopsticks. The tool comes before the object, and the object keeps its を.
texts.Method and tool both use the same word d: Method and tool both use the same word で, so the sentences look alike. The noun tells you which one it is. A language, a phone or a TV is a method. Something you hold in your hand, like はし, えんぴつ or スプーン, is a tool. で therefore has three jobs in this chapter: place (どこで), method (どうやって or なにで) and tool (なにで). A quick test is to ask the question. Where does it happen? That is place. How do you do it? That is method. What do you use? That is tool.
texts.Two patterns hide in the samples. A leng: Two patterns hide in the samples. A length of time, such as いちねんかん or じゅうごふん, takes no marker at all. And いっしゅうかん に いっかい uses に to mean per, so it reads once per week. You met that how-often pattern in Chapter 5.
texts.A question word replaces the part you wa: A question word replaces the part you want to know, and it keeps the same marker its answer will take. If the answer takes を, the question is なにを. If the answer takes で for a place, the question is どこで. Swap the question word for the real answer and the marker stays where it is.
texts.Dare means who, and donata is the polite: だれ means who, and どなた is the polite version. なに で and どうやって both ask how, and なにで also asks what tool. You ask a tool question with なにで and a language question with どうやって or なにで. The book lists these question words in a table, and then gives seven pairs of a question and its answer. The first six rows are the table, and the pairs follow.
texts.The five short conversations on page 124: The five short conversations on page 124 give you real-life lines that use the patterns of this chapter. Each row below is one line, and the English column shows who says it: アナ and Mari in the first, second and last conversations, and キム and Ben in the other two.
texts.A few small words are worth knowing. Jou: A few small words are worth knowing. じょうず means good at, and にほんごが じょうずですね is a compliment. A modest reply is いいえ、まだまだです, which means no, not yet. どのぐらい asks how long, and いくら ぐらい asks about how much. どう でした か asks how something was. The little word よ at the end of a sentence adds a friendly you know, and ね asks for agreement, as in そうですね. ちょっと before むずかしい makes it a little difficult.
texts.Look for the markers as you read. Doko d: Look for the markers as you read. どこ で にほんご を べんきょうしましたか has どこで for the place and を for the object, and パンと くだものです uses to to mean and. In the second conversation the book notes that にほんご が じょうず です means good at にほんご, and まだまだ means not yet.
texts.Most nouns in this chapter only fit one: Most nouns in this chapter only fit one or two verbs, so learning them in pairs saves a lot of effort. たべます goes with food: あさごはん, ひるごはん, ばんごはん, ごはん, ラーメン and pan. のみます goes with drinks, including みず, おちゃ, こうちゃ, ぎゅうにゅう, コーヒー, コーラ, ジュース, おさけ, ビール, ワイン, スープ and くすり (medicine).
texts.Yomimasu goes with reading materials: sh: よみます goes with reading materials: しょうせつ, ざっし, しんぶん and ほん. ききます goes with おんがく and うた, and みます goes with ニュース, えいが and テレビ. かきます goes with レポート, メール and てがみ. うたいます goes with うた, すいます with タバコ and かけます with でんわ. かいます and うります are opposites and can take almost any thing.
texts.Hanashimasu and oshiemasu work different: はなします and おしえます work differently. はなします usually takes a person with と or に, or a language with で. おしえます takes a person with に and a subject with を. When you are not sure which verb a noun needs, think about what you do with it: you eat food, drink a drink and read a text.
texts.de has three jobs in this chapter. Place: で has three jobs in this chapter. Place: きっさてん で (at the coffee shop). Method: えいご で (in English). Tool: はし で (with chopsticks).
texts.Ask the question to sort them out. doko: Ask the question to sort them out. どこで is place, どうやって is method and なにで is tool.
texts.Do not put no before de: say eigo de, ne: Do not put no before で: say えいご で, never えいご の で.

texts.de goes with an action verb: kaisha de h: で goes with an action verb: かいしゃで はたらきます (work at the company).
texts.ni goes with imasu and arimasu: kaisha n: に goes with います and あります: かいしゃに います (be at the company).
texts.Ask yourself whether something happens t: Ask yourself whether something happens there (で) or someone is there (に).
texts.ni is for the person who receives the ac: に is for the person who receives the action: ともだちに でんわを かけます (call a friend).
texts.to is for the person who does it with yo: to is for the person who does it with you: ともだち と えいがを みます (watch a movie with a friend).
texts.hanashimasu can take both: shachou to ha: はなします can take both: しゃちょうと はなしました (spoke with) and おかあさんに はなしました (spoke to).
texts.issho ni goes with to, as in ane to issh: いっしょに goes with to, as in あね to いっしょに.
texts.After a person and right before the verb: After a person and right before the verb, と means with: かぞく と たべました。
texts.Between two nouns, to means and: pan to: Between two nouns, と means and: パン と くだもの (bread and fruit).
texts.O or wa in a negative sentence: O or は in a negative sentence
を is neutral: しょうせつ を よみません。
texts.wa puts the spotlight on the thing you d: は puts the spotlight on the thing you do not do: ワインは のみません (wine is the thing I skip).
texts.Both are correct. wa is common when you: Both are correct. は is common when you compare two things.
texts.The object marker is written を but sound: The object marker is written を but sounds like を. The topic marker is written は but sounds like は.
texts.A specific time takes ni: nichiyoubi ni,: A specific time takes に: にちようび に, くじ に。
texts.Non-specific words take no ni: maiasa, m: Non-specific words take no に: まいあさ, まいばん, まいにち, まいしゅう, けさ and きのう。
から, まで and ごろ never take に.
texts.A length of time takes no marker at all:: A length of time takes no marker at all: いちねんかん べんきょうしました。
texts.isshuukan ni ikkai is different, because: いっしゅうかん に いっかい is different, because に means per there.
texts.goro is around a point in time: kuji gor: ごろ is around a point in time: くじ ごろ (around 9 o'clock).
texts.gurai is about an amount: nijikan gurai: ぐらい is about an amount: にじかん ぐらい (about 2 hours), じゅうまん えん ぐらい (about 100,000 yen).
texts.donogurai and ikura gurai ask about an a: どのぐらい and いくら ぐらい ask about an amount, so they use ぐらい.
texts.Kikimasu: listen or ask: ききます: listen or ask
texts.A thing with o means listen: ongaku o ki: A thing with を means listen: おんがくを ききます.
texts.A person with ni means ask: sensei ni ki: A person with に means ask: せんせい に ききます。
texts.Hanashimasu with three markers: はなします with three markers
texts.A person with to means talk with: shacho: A person with と means talk with: しゃちょう と はなします。
texts.A person with ni means talk to: okaasan: A person with に means talk to: おかあさん に はなします。
texts.A language with de means speak in it: ei: A language with で means speak in it: えいごで はなします.
texts.mimasu means watch, look or see: eiga o: みます means watch, look or see: えいがを みます, ニュースを みます.
texts.Kakimasu, kaimasu and kakemasu: かきます, かいます and かけます
かきます is write: メール を かきます。
かいます is buy: くつを かいます.
かけます is call: でんわを かけます.
texts.Mimasu, nomimasu and yomimasu: みます, のみます and よみます
All three end in みます.
texts.mimasu is watch, nomimasu is drink and y: みます is watch, のみます is drink and よみます is read.
texts.Think of the object: eiga, mizu, shinbun: Think of the object: えいが, みず, しんぶん。
texts.Kikimasu and kakimasu: ききます and かきます
texts.Only the first sound changes. Kiki is li: Only the first sound changes. きき is listen or ask, and かき is write.
texts.Kaimasu, urimasu and utaimasu: かいます, うります and うたいます
texts.kaimasu is buy and urimasu is sell, so t: かいます is buy and うります is sell, so they are opposites.
texts.urimasu (sell) and utaimasu (sing) both: うります (sell) and うたいます (sing) both start with う.
texts.uta is a song and utaimasu is to sing. Y: うた is a song and うたいます is to sing. You sing a song: うたを うたいます.
おちゃ is tea and こうちゃ is black tea.
texts.gohan is a meal or cooked rice. Add asa,: ごはん is a meal or cooked rice. Add あさ, ひる or ban to say which meal.
texts.osake is alcohol in general. bi-ru and w: おさけ is alcohol in general. ビール and ワイン are two kinds of it.
texts.tabemono, nomimono and yomimono all end: たべもの, のみもの and よみもの all end in もの, which means thing. They are things to eat, to drink and to read.
texts.Zenzen and the time words: ぜんぜん and the time words
texts.zenzen always needs a negative ending: z: ぜんぜん always needs a negative ending: ぜんぜん のみません。
texts.itsumo, tokidoki and mainichi go with a: いつも, ときどき and まいにち go with a positive verb: ときどき のみます。
texts.ototoi and yuube are in the past, so the: おととい and ゆうべ are in the past, so the verb ends in ました or ません でした。
texts.nani o is what, doko de is where, dare n: なにを is what, どこで is where, だれ に is to whom, だれ to is with whom, どうやって is how and なにで is with what tool.
どなた is the polite form of だれ.
texts.Eiga and eigakan: えいが and えいがかん
texts.eiga is a movie and eigakan is a movie t: えいが is a movie and えいがかん is a movie theater.
texts.You watch a movie (eiga o mimasu) at the: You watch a movie (えいがを みます) at the theater (えいがかん で).
texts.hayai (early, fast), hatarakimasu (work): はやい (early, fast), はたらきます (work), はじまります (start), はなします (speak), はし (chopsticks), はなみ (flower viewing) and はなび (fireworks) all start with は.
texts.hanashimasu starts like hana (flower) bu: はなします starts like はな (flower) but has nothing to do with it. Only はなみ and はなび are about flowers.
texts.yasui (cheap), yasumimasu (rest), hiruya: やすい (cheap), やすみます (rest), ひるやすみ (lunch break) and やさしい (kind, easy) share やす. やすい is about price, やすみ is about resting and やさしい is about people and easy things.
texts.Many words start with o. Sort them by ty: Many words start with を. Sort them by type: おきます, おわります and おしえます are verbs, おそい, おもい, おもしろい, おおきい and おいしい are adjectives, and おちゃ and おさけ are drinks.
texts.Katakana is for words borrowed from othe: Katakana is for words borrowed from other languages, and most of the katakana words in Chapters 6 to 8 come from English: ベッド, テスト, メール, レポート, コーヒー, ジュース, ビール, ワイン, スプーン and ニュース。
texts.A few do not. ra-men comes from Chinese,: A few do not. ラーメン comes from Chinese, pan (bread) and タバコ (cigarette) come from Portuguese, and カラオケ mixes Japanese and English.
texts.biru (building) and bi-ru (beer) differ: ビル (building) and ビール (beer) differ only in the long vowel, so watch the dash.

texts.9.1 Destination e or ni, and origin kara: 9.1 Destination へ or に, and origin から きました (ぶんけい 9.1)
texts.Chapter 9 is about moving from one place: Chapter 9 is about moving from one place to another. The first pattern says where someone goes. It is A は destination へ or に, followed by a motion verb. The four motion verbs are いきます (go), きます (come), かえります (go home or return) and もどります (go back).
texts.After the place you can use e or ni, and: After the place you can use へ or に, and the book says the two are interchangeable. E stresses the direction, as in heading toward a place. に stresses the point where you arrive. The marker へ is written へ in kana, but it is read へ, not he. Do not mix it up with the に that marks a time, as in くじ に (at nine o'clock). After a place word, に means to.
texts.Kaerimasu and modorimasu both mean to re: かえります and もどります both mean to return, but they are not the same. かえります is going home, to the place where you live or belong, such as your house or your home country. もどります is going back to a place you were at before, such as a station or an office.
texts.To say where someone comes from, use pla: To say where someone comes from, use place + から + きました. フランス から きました is I came from France. から きました is a set phrase, and it answers the question どこから きました か (where did you come from).
9.2 Mode of transportation で (ぶんけい 9.2)
texts.Put de after a vehicle to say how you tr: Put で after a vehicle to say how you travel. じてんしゃ で is by bicycle, バス で is by bus and でんしゃ で is by train. The pattern is vehicle + で + motion verb. The one exception is あるいて, which means on foot or by walking. It already carries the meaning of by, so it takes no で.
texts.This de is not the place de from Chapter: This で is not the place で from Chapter 8. In Chapter 8, で marked the place where an action happens, as in としょかんで べんきょうしました (I studied at the library). Here で marks the vehicle you use to get somewhere. A quick check: if the word before で is a vehicle, で means by.
texts.With a motion verb, the place you head t: With a motion verb, the place you head to takes へ or に, never で. Compare the last two rows. うみ へ いきます is I go to the sea, because いきます is a motion verb. うみ で およぎます is I swim in the sea, because およぎます is an activity at a place.
texts.The question words for a vehicle are nan: The question words for a vehicle are なにで and どうやって, and both mean how.
texts.9.3 Time words ni, kara, made and goro (: 9.3 Time words に, から, まで and ごろ (ぶんけい 9.3)
texts.The time markers you met in Chapters 7 a: The time markers you met in Chapters 7 and 8 work the same way with motion verbs. に marks one exact time, such as a clock time, a day of the week or a date. から means from and まで means until, so くじ から ごじ まで is from 9 until 5. ごろ means around, and it goes straight after the time with no に.
texts.Words that are not an exact time take no: Words that are not an exact time take no に. These include きのう, ゆうべ, おとといの よる and まいとし (every year). You say まいとし フィリピン へ いきます, never まいとし に.
texts.The second row has ni (wa) after kusuriy: The second row has に (は) after くすりや. The は in brackets is optional. It puts the spotlight on that one place, the same trick as を and は in the negative sentences of Chapter 8. So くすりや に は いきませんでした says I did not go to the drugstore, at least, and it hints that you went to other places.
texts.Time words that point to the past, like: Time words that point to the past, like きのう, ゆうべ and おととい, go with ました or ません でした. Watch the two jobs of から. After a place, as in にほん から, it means from a place. After a time, as in くじ から, it means from a start time, and it goes with まで.
texts.9.4 Companion to or issho ni (bunkei 9.4: 9.4 Companion と or いっしょに (ぶんけい 9.4)
texts.The pattern is person + to (or to issho: The pattern is person + to (or to いっしょに) + verb. It names the person who goes, comes or returns together with you. いっしょ に only stresses the word together, so ともだち to いきます and ともだち to いっしょに いきます mean the same thing.
texts.This is the same to as in Chapter 8, whe: This is the same to as in Chapter 8, where it also meant with. Remember that to has a second job: between two nouns or two places it means and. In スーパーと ぎんこうへ いきました, と means and. The way to tell them apart is the position. A to that comes right after a person and right before the verb means with.
texts.For your own family, use the plain words: For your own family, use the plain words such as はは and あね. For someone else's family, use the polite words such as おかあさん and おねえさん. The questions are だれ to and the more polite どなた to, both meaning with whom.
texts.9.5 Counter for people de (bunkei 9.5): 9.5 Counter for people で (ぶんけい 9.5)
texts.The pattern is number of people + de + v: The pattern is number of people + で + verb. It says how many of you do something together. The count includes you, so ふたり で means two people in all, you and one other person. ひとり で means alone, by yourself.
texts.This de marks the size of a group. It is: This で marks the size of a group. It is a third job for で, after the place で of Chapter 8 and the vehicle で of 9.2. The word before で tells you which one it is: a place, a vehicle or a number of people.
The rows start with the people counters. One and two people are special words, ひとり and ふたり. From three on it is the number plus にん: さんにん, よにん, ごにん and so on. Four is よにん, never しにん. Seven can be しちにん or ななにん. なんにん asks how many people. After the counters come the book's eight sample sentences.
texts.A question word takes the same marker it: A question word takes the same marker its answer will take. Swap the question word for the real answer and the marker stays where it is. The book lists four question words for motion verbs. どこ へ or どこ に asks where to. なに で or どうやって asks how, which means the vehicle. だれ to or the polite どなた to asks with whom. なんにん で asks how many people.
texts.Two more question words are not on the b: Two more question words are not on the book's list, but they are natural partners of the same markers. どこ から asks where from, and なんじごろ asks around what time. They are the first six rows. After them come the book's five question and answer pairs.
texts.Read each pair and spot the marker. In t: Read each pair and spot the marker. In the pair about the party, なんにんで is answered by さんにん で, so the counter takes the same で.
texts.Ne at the end of a sentence asks the oth: ね at the end of a sentence asks the other person to agree with you. Think of it as isn't it, right or don't you think. Use it when you expect a yes, as in きのう あつかったですね. The usual reply is そうですね, which means yes, I agree.
texts.Ne is not a question word, so it does no: ね is not a question word, so it does not need か after it. はい or ええ in front of the reply just means yes. In the table below, the English column shows who says each line: A starts and B replies.
texts.Yo at the end of a sentence adds emphasi: よ at the end of a sentence adds emphasis. It says this is the answer and I am telling you. It is good for correcting someone, as in いいえ、インドじんですよ, or for giving news the other person may not know, as in かいしゃの レポートを かきましたよ.
texts.Here is a quick test to tell yo and ne a: Here is a quick test to tell よ and ね apart. ね asks the listener to nod. よ tells the listener something. Use ね when you are sure they will agree, and よ when you are adding or fixing information.
texts.9.9 Masu form and dictionary form: two f: 9.9 ます form and dictionary form: two forms of every verb
texts.Every verb has two forms. So far you hav: Every verb has two forms. So far you have used the formal one, which ends in ます. The other is the dictionary form, the one you look up in a dictionary. It sounds casual, so the book also calls it the informal form. The meaning is the same, and only the politeness changes. Compare おんがくを ききます with おんがくを きく.
texts.If you cut masu off a formal verb, what: If you cut ます off a formal verb, what is left is the stem. The book calls it the pre-ます form or the stem form. For のみます the stem is のみ. The stem is the middle step when you change from one form to the other.
texts.The book sorts every verb into one of th: The book sorts every verb into one of three types, and the names are the book's own. Irregular verbs have a stem that ends in an い sound, and the last sound shifts when the form changes, as in のみます and かきます. Regular verbs have a stem that ends in へ, and you only add or drop る, as in たべます. Special verbs have fixed forms that you simply memorize, and they are します (do) and きます (come). Other books call the book's irregular verbs う-verbs and its regular verbs る-verbs. The names differ, but the verbs are the same.

texts.To go from the masu form to the dictiona: To go from the ます form to the dictionary form, you first remove ます to get the stem. What you do next depends on the type.
texts.For Irregular verbs, change the last sou: For Irregular verbs, change the last sound of the stem from the い row to the う row. のみ becomes のむ, and かき becomes かく. The table below shows every shift: み と む, き と く, ぎ と ぐ, し と す, ち と つ, い と う, に と ぬ, び と ぶ and り to る. Notice that ち becomes つ and not ちゅ. For Regular verbs, add る to the stem. たべ becomes たべる, and み becomes みる. Special verbs have no steps, so します is always する and きます is always くる.
texts.There is a catch when you go in this dir: There is a catch when you go in this direction. A few Regular verbs also end in います, such as みます and おきます. From the ます form alone you cannot always tell, so learn those as pairs. And かえります looks like it could be Regular, but it is Irregular, so the dictionary form is かえる.
speak. Irregular: し changes to す.
wait. Irregular: ち changes to つ.
eat. Regular: remove ます and add る.
watch. Regular: remove ます and add る.
texts.wake up. It ends in imasu but it is Regu: wake up. It ends in います but it is Regular, so just add る.
texts.9.11 From dictionary form to masu form (: 9.11 From dictionary form to ます form (page 138)
texts.Going the other way, from the dictionary: Going the other way, from the dictionary form to the ます form, you look at the ending of the dictionary form first.
texts.Irregular verbs end in bu, mu, nu, gu, s: Irregular verbs end in ぶ, む, ぬ, ぐ, す, く, う, つ, or る after a, う or を. Change the last sound from the う row to the い row, and then add ます. のむ becomes のみ, and then のみます. The book's step box leaves out う and つ, but its table on the next page includes them, so かう becomes かいます and まつ becomes まちます.
texts.Regular verbs end in eru or iru. Remove: Regular verbs end in える or いる. Remove る and add ます. たべる becomes たべ, and then たべます. Special verbs are fixed: する is します and くる is きます.
texts.The big trap is kaeru. It ends in eru li: The big trap is かえる. It ends in える like a Regular verb, but it follows the Irregular rule, so it is かえります. The book names はいる (enter), はしる (run), きる (cut) and しる (know) as the same kind of trap.
texts.drink. Irregular: mu changes to mi, then: drink. Irregular: む changes to み, then add ます.
texts.write. Irregular: ku changes to ki, then: write. Irregular: く changes to き, then add ます.
texts.swim. Irregular: gu changes to gi, then: swim. Irregular: ぐ changes to ぎ, then add ます.
texts.speak. Irregular: su changes to shi, the: speak. Irregular: す changes to し, then add ます.
texts.wait. Irregular: tsu changes to chi, the: wait. Irregular: つ changes to ち, then add ます.
texts.buy. Irregular: u changes to i, then add: buy. Irregular: う changes to い, then add ます.
texts.die. Irregular: nu changes to ni, then a: die. Irregular: ぬ changes to に, then add ます.
texts.play. Irregular: bu changes to bi, then: play. Irregular: ぶ changes to び, then add ます.
texts.understand. Irregular: ru changes to ri,: understand. Irregular: る changes to り, then add ます.
eat. Regular: remove る and add ます.
watch. Regular: remove る and add ます.
texts.go home. The trap: it ends in eru but it: go home. The trap: it ends in える but it is Irregular, so it is かえります and not かえます.
texts.To help you sort verbs, the book groups: To help you sort verbs, the book groups them by the last sound of the dictionary form, which is the present positive informal form. The Irregular verbs are split into five groups. Group 1 ends in ぶ, む or ぬ. Group 2 ends in ぐ. Group 3 ends in す. Group 4 ends in く. Group 5 covers everything else: う, つ and る after a, う or を.
texts.The Regular verbs end in eru or iru, and: The Regular verbs end in える or いる, and the Special verbs are する and くる. Each row below shows the dictionary form first and then the ます form.
texts.The book puts a star on iku and kaeru in: The book puts a star on いく and かえる in Group 5. Its note says the starred verbs are exceptions, along with しる (know), はいる (enter), はしる (run), きる (cut) and so on. かえる is the real trap, because it ends in える but acts like an Irregular verb. The book does not say why いく is starred. Its ます form follows the normal く rule, so いく becomes いきます.
texts.eat. Regular, ends in eru: eat. Regular, ends in える
texts.watch. Regular, ends in iru: watch. Regular, ends in いる
texts.The four motion verbs follow the same fo: The four motion verbs follow the same four endings as every other ます verb: ます, ません, ました and ません でした. いきます becomes いきません, いきました and いきませんでした. きます becomes きません, きました and きませんでした。 かえります and もどります work in the same way. The first 16 rows show all of them.
texts.There is one split that matters a lot. V: There is one split that matters a lot. Verbs of going use へ or に for the place you head to. Activity verbs, namely あそびます (play), およぎます (swim) and かいものします (shop), use で for the place where you do the activity. The last six rows put the two side by side. If you are unsure which marker と use, ask yourself whether you are moving to the place or doing something at the place.
texts.The Special verbs include every noun + s: The Special verbs include every noun + します verb, such as べんきょうします and かいものします. Their dictionary forms just swap します for する. Watch out for かえります, which looks Regular but is Irregular, and for みます and おきます, which end in います but are Regular.
texts.Watch the markers as you read. Ryokou o: Watch the markers as you read. りょこう を しました uses を with します, so it means took a trip. かかります is a new verb that means takes, as in takes time, and it goes with a length of time that has no marker. しゅっぱつ は しがつ とおか です uses は to make the departure the topic, and the date is simply the answer.
texts.E or ni after a place, ni after a time: E or に after a place, に after a time
texts.After a place word, e and ni both mean t: After a place word, へ and に both mean to: うみへ いきます or うみ に いきます (go to the sea).
texts.After a time word, ni means at or on: ku: After a time word, に means at or on: くじ に いきます (go at nine o'clock).
texts.The two ni look the same but do differen: The two に look the same but do different jobs. Ask yourself whether the word before it is a place or a time.
texts.e stresses the direction. ni stresses th: へ stresses the direction. に stresses the point where you arrive. In everyday speech they are interchangeable.
texts.E or de with a place: E or で with a place
texts.Going to a place takes e or ni: umi e ik: Going to a place takes へ or に: うみへ いきます (go to the sea).
texts.Doing something at a place takes de: umi: Doing something at a place takes で: うみで およぎます (swim in the sea).
texts.Ask whether the verb moves you to the pl: Ask whether the verb moves you to the place or whether the action happens there. Motion verbs take へ. Activity verbs take で.
texts.kaimonoshimasu, asobimasu, oyogimasu and: かいものします, あそびます, およぎます and べんきょうします are activity verbs, so they take で.
texts.De for a vehicle, de for a number of peo: で for a vehicle, で for a number of people
texts.Look at the word before de. A vehicle sa: Look at the word before で. A vehicle says how you travel: バス で (by bus).
texts.A number of people says how many of you: A number of people says how many of you go: さんにん で (three of us).
texts.Both can be in one sentence: sannin de b: Both can be in one sentence: さんにん で バス で いきます (the three of us go by bus).
texts.aruite (on foot) already says how you tr: あるいて (on foot) already says how you travel, so it never takes で.
texts.to right before the verb means with: tom: to right before the verb means with: ともだち と いきます (go with a friend).
texts.to between two places or nouns means and: to between two places or nouns means and: スーパーと ぎんこうへ いきました (went to the supermarket and the bank).
texts.issho ni backs up the with meaning: tomo: いっしょに backs up the with meaning: ともだち to いっしょに いきます. いっしょに alone never replaces to.
texts.Kara for a place, kara for a time: から for a place, から for a time
texts.A place plus kara plus kimashita means c: A place plus から plus きました means came from: フランスから きました (came from France).
texts.A time plus kara plus made means from an: A time plus から plus まで means from and until: くじ から ごじ まで (from nine to five).
texts.kara and made also work with places: shi: から and まで also work with places: シンガポール から マレーシア まで (from Singapore to Malaysia).
texts.An exact time or a day takes ni: kuji ni: An exact time or a day takes に: くじ に, げつようび に, じゅうにがつ にじゅうごにち に。
texts.Habit and relative words take no ni: kin: Habit and relative words take no に: きのう, ゆうべ, おととい, まいとし, こんげつ, せんげつ, らいしゅう, こんばん and ことし。
texts.goro never takes ni: sanji goro kimashit: ごろ never takes に: さんじ ごろ きました (came around three).
texts.A length of time takes no marker at all:: A length of time takes no marker at all: バスで さんじかん かかります (it takes three hours by bus).
texts.The marker e is read e: The marker へ is read え
texts.The marker is written with the kana for: The marker is written with the kana for he, but it is read へ.
texts.nihon e ikimasu is read nihon e ikimasu,: にほん へ いきます is read にほん へ いきます, never にほん he いきます.
texts.The same thing happens with wa (written: The same thing happens with は (written with the kana for は) and を (written with the kana for を).
texts.Inside a word the kana still says he. he: Inside a word the kana still says へ. へんじ (reply) and へや (room) start with へ.
texts.Ikimasu and kimasu: いきます and きます
texts.ikimasu is go and kimasu is come. They t: いきます is go and きます is come. They take the same markers.
texts.Only the direction changes: watashi wa n: Only the direction changes: わたしは にほんへ いきます (I go to Japan) and ともだち は いえ へ きました (my friend came to my house).
texts.kara goes with kimashita when you say wh: から goes with きました when you say where you came from.
texts.Ikimasu and imasu: いきます and います
texts.ikimasu is go. imasu is to be somewhere,: いきます is go. います is to be somewhere, used for people and animals.
texts.imasu appears in the readings, as in shi: います appears in the readings, as in シンガポール に います (be in Singapore).
texts.Kaerimasu or modorimasu: かえります or もどります
texts.kaerimasu is go home, to where you live: かえります is go home, to where you live or belong: にほん へ かえります (go home to Japan).
texts.modorimasu is go back to a place you wer: もどります is go back to a place you were at before, such as a station or an office: えき に もどります。
texts.Both are fine for return. kaerimasu is t: Both are fine for return. かえります is the one you will use most.
texts.Kaerimasu, kaimasu and kakemasu: かえります, かいます and かけます
texts.kaerimasu is go home, kaimasu is buy and: かえります is go home, かいます is buy and かけます is call (a phone).
texts.Check the markers: a place with e goes w: Check the markers: a place with へ goes with かえります, a thing with を goes with かいます, and でんわ を goes with かけます.
texts.Kimasu, kikimasu and kirimasu: きます, ききます and きります
texts.kimasu is come, kikimasu is listen or as: きます is come, ききます is listen or ask, and きります is cut.
texts.kimasu is a Special verb. kikimasu and k: きます is a Special verb. ききます and きります are Irregular verbs.
texts.In the dictionary form they are kuru, ki: In the dictionary form they are くる, きく and きる. Do not mix up くる and きる。
texts.Asobimasu and oyogimasu: あそびます and およぎます
texts.Both are activity verbs, so they take de: Both are activity verbs, so they take で for the place.
texts.asobimasu is play or enjoy yourself, and: あそびます is play or enjoy yourself, and およぎます is swim.
texts.kouen de asobimasu (play in the park) an: こうえんで あそびます (play in the park) and うみで およぎます (swim in the sea).
texts.hitori (1) and futari (2) are special wo: ひとり (1) and ふたり (2) are special words.
texts.From three on it is the number plus nin:: From three on it is the number plus にん: さんにん, よにん, ごにん, ろくにん, はちにん, きゅうにん, じゅうにん。
texts.Four is yonin, never shinin. Seven is sh: Four is よにん, never しにん. Seven is しちにん or ななにん。
texts.The count includes you. futari de is two: The count includes you. ふたり で is two people in all, and ひとりで is alone.
texts.For how many people, say nannin de ikima: For how many people, say なんにんで いきました か.
texts.goro is around a point in time: kuji gor: ごろ is around a point in time: くじ ごろ (around nine o'clock).
texts.gurai is about an amount of time: sanjik: ぐらい is about an amount of time: さんじかん ぐらい (about three hours).
texts.goro goes with a clock time, and gurai g: ごろ goes with a clock time, and ぐらい goes with a length of time.
texts.nanji goro asks around what time. nanjik: なんじごろ asks around what time. なんじかん ぐらい asks about how long.
texts.Nani de or douyatte: なに で or どうやって
texts.Both ask how you travel, and both are an: Both ask how you travel, and both are answered with a vehicle plus で.
texts.nani de ikimasu ka and douyatte ikimasu: なにで いきます か and どうやっていきますか get the same answer: バス で いきます。
texts.dare to asks with whom, and nannin de as: だれ to asks with whom, and なんにんで asks how many people.
texts.doko e asks where to. It has the same jo: どこへ asks where to. It has the same job as どこ に.
texts.ne asks the other person to agree: atsui: ね asks the other person to agree: あつい です ね (it is hot, isn't it?).
texts.yo tells the other person something, or: よ tells the other person something, or stresses it: インドじん です よ (I am Indian, you know).
texts.The usual reply to ne is sou desu ne, wh: The usual reply to ね is そうですね, which means yes, I agree.
texts.yo can also correct someone: iie, asatte: よ can also correct someone: いいえ, あさって です よ (no, it is the day after tomorrow!).
texts.Masu form and dictionary form: ます form and dictionary form
texts.The masu form is formal. The dictionary: The ます form is formal. The dictionary form is casual, and it is the form you look up in a dictionary.
texts.The stem is what is left when you remove: The stem is what is left when you remove ます. のみます has the stem のみ.
texts.Check the dictionary form first. A verb: Check the dictionary form first. A verb that ends in える or いる is probably Regular.
texts.Every other ending (bu, mu, nu, gu, su,: Every other ending (ぶ, む, ぬ, ぐ, す, く, う, つ, る after a, う or を) is Irregular.
texts.suru and kuru are Special, and so is a n: する and くる are Special, and so is a noun plus する, such as べんきょうする.
texts.Traps: eru or iru that is not Regular: Traps: える or いる that is not Regular
かえる ends in える, but it is Irregular. It becomes かえります, never かえます.
texts.The book names hairu, hashiru, kiru and: The book names はいる, はしる, きる and しる as the same kind of trap.
texts.Learn them as pairs: kaeru and kaerimasu: Learn them as pairs: かえる and かえります, はいる and はいります。
texts.Traps: ending in imasu but Regular: Traps: ending in います but Regular
texts.mimasu and okimasu end in imasu, but the: みます and おきます end in います, but they are Regular verbs.
texts.Just add ru: mimasu becomes miru, and ok: Just add る: みます becomes みる, and おきます becomes おきる.
texts.From the masu form alone you cannot alwa: From the ます form alone you cannot always tell, so learn those two as pairs.
texts.A verb ending in u changes u to i before: A verb ending in う changes う to い before ます: すう becomes すいます and かう becomes かいます.
texts.A verb ending in tsu changes tsu to chi:: A verb ending in つ changes つ to ち: まつ becomes まちます.
texts.A verb ending in nu changes nu to ni: sh: A verb ending in ぬ changes ぬ to に: しぬ becomes しにます.
texts.A verb ending in su changes su to shi: h: A verb ending in す changes す to し: はなす becomes はなします.
texts.Iku is starred in the book: いく is starred in the book
texts.The book puts a star on iku, in the same: The book puts a star on いく, in the same note as かえる and しる。
texts.The rule still works for iku: ku changes: The rule still works for いく: く changes to き, so you get いきます.
texts.kaeru is the real trap. iku does not cat: かえる is the real trap. いく does not catch you out.
texts.kaerimasu means go home or return: nihon: かえります means go home or return: にほん へ かえります。
texts.hayai means fast or early: takushi- wa h: はやい means fast or early: タクシー は はやいですよ (the taxi is fast).
texts.kakarimasu means takes (time): gojikan k: かかります means takes (time): ごじかん かかります (it takes five hours).
texts.kinou, yuube, ototoi, sengetsu and kyone: きのう, ゆうべ, おととい, せんげつ and きょねん point to the past.
texts.The verb then ends in mashita or masen d: The verb then ends in ました or ません でした。
texts.ashita, raishuu, raigetsu and konban poi: あした, らいしゅう, らいげつ and こんばん point to the present or future, so the verb ends in ます or ません。
texts.bijutsukan, eigakan and toshokan all end: びじゅつかん, えいがかん and としょかん all end in かん, a building: museum, movie theater and library.
texts.ryokan is a Japanese style inn. ryokou i: りょかん is a Japanese style inn. りょこう is a trip.
texts.inaka, machi and mura are the countrysid: いなか, まち and むら are the countryside, a town and a village.
texts.kawa, ike and umi are a river, a pond an: かわ, いけ and うみ are a river, a pond and the sea.
texts.gaikoku is a foreign country. kaigai is: がいこく is a foreign country. かいがい is overseas.
texts.otera and onsen are a temple and a hot s: おてら and おんせん are a temple and a hot spring.
texts.kaimonoshimasu: present negative: かいものします: present negative
texts.kimasen deshita: past positive: きませんでした: past positive
texts.kaerimasen: past negative: かえりません: past negative
texts.modorimashita: present negative: もどりました: present negative
texts.oyogimasen deshita: およぎません でした
