texts.10.1 Noun + suru (bunkei 10.1, page 148): 10.1 Noun + する (ぶんけい 10.1, page 148)
texts.Many actions in Japanese are said with a: Many actions in Japanese are said with a noun plus する. The noun names the action, and する does the job of the verb, much like the English word do. The noun べんきょう means study, and べんきょうします is the verb to study. The formal form is します, and the casual form, which you meet later in this chapter, is する.
texts.The book writes the noun and shimasu tog: The book writes the noun and します together as one word, as in うんてんします (drive) and そうじします (clean). The ending behaves just like します, so you get しません, しました and しません でした. Other markers work as usual. The person you do something to takes に, as in かちょうに せつめいしました. The thing you do something to takes を, as in へや を そうじします.
texts.Sports and games also take suru. For exa: Sports and games also take する. For example, テニスしました means played tennis, and ゴルフします means play golf. Do not use あそびます for a sport. The list below shows every noun + する verb in the book, and then the book's example sentences.
texts.In Chapter 7 you learned four formal ver: In Chapter 7 you learned four formal verb endings: ます, ません, ました and ません でした. Every verb also has four informal forms. They mean the same thing, but they sound more casual, and you use them with family, close friends and people your own age or younger. With a teacher, a boss or someone you have just met, keep using the formal forms.
texts.The four informal forms have names in th: The four informal forms have names in the book. The present positive is the dictionary form, which you learned in Chapter 9. The present negative is the ない form. The past positive is the た form. The past negative is the なかった form. For おわる (finish) they are おわる, おわらない, おわった and おわらなかった。
texts.The way each form is made depends on the: The way each form is made depends on the type of verb. The book has three types: Irregular verbs (the book's name for the verbs that end in う in the dictionary form, such as のむ), Regular verbs (the ones that end in える or いる, such as たべる) and Special verbs (する and くる). The Irregular verbs are split into five groups, and the next lessons go through them one by one. In every group the present negative ends in ない, the past positive ends in た or だ, and the past negative is the ない form with the last い changed to かった.
texts.will not finish (informal, nai form): will not finish (informal, ない form)
texts.did not finish (informal, nakatta form): did not finish (informal, なかった form)
texts.10.3 Group 1: verbs that end in bu, mu o: 10.3 Group 1: verbs that end in ぶ, む or ぬ (page 149)
texts.Group 1 has the verbs whose dictionary f: Group 1 has the verbs whose dictionary form ends in ぶ, む or ぬ. To make the ない form, change the last う sound と the a sound and add ない: ぶ becomes ば, む becomes ま, and ぬ becomes な. So あそぶ becomes あそばない, のむ becomes のまない, and しぬ becomes しなない.
texts.For the ta form, bu, mu and nu all chang: For the た form, ぶ, む and ぬ all change to the same ending, んだ. So あそぶ becomes あそんだ, のむ becomes のんだ, and しぬ becomes しんだ. The past negative takes the ない form and changes ない to なかった, so you get あそばなかった, のまなかった and しななかった。
texts.Because so many verbs end in nda, the ta: Because so many verbs end in んだ, the た form alone does not tell you the dictionary form. A form such as よんだ could come from よむ (read) or from よぶ (call), so context decides.
texts.10.4 Group 2: verbs that end in gu (page: 10.4 Group 2: verbs that end in ぐ (page 149)
texts.Group 2 has the verbs that end in gu. Th: Group 2 has the verbs that end in ぐ. The verb およぐ (swim) is the only one of this group in your vocabulary. For the ない form, ぐ becomes が plus ない, so およぐ becomes およがない.
texts.The ta form is different from Group 1. T: The た form is different from Group 1. The ending ぐ changes to いだ, so およぐ becomes およいだ. Do not say およいんだ or およんだ. The past negative is およがなかった.
texts.10.5 Group 3: verbs that end in su (page: 10.5 Group 3: verbs that end in す (page 149)
texts.Group 3 has the verbs that end in su, su: Group 3 has the verbs that end in す, such as はなす (speak) and だす (submit). For the ない form, す becomes さ plus ない, as in はなさない and ださない。
texts.The ta form changes su to shita. So hana: The た form changes す to した. So はなす becomes はなした, and だす becomes だした. Notice that はなした looks like the た form of する (した, did), but the verb here is はなす and the sound はな comes first. The past negative is はなさなかった.
texts.10.6 Group 4: verbs that end in ku (page: 10.6 Group 4: verbs that end in く (page 149)
texts.Group 4 has the verbs that end in ku, su: Group 4 has the verbs that end in く, such as かく (write), きく (listen or ask), はたらく (work) and あるく (walk). For the ない form, く becomes か plus ない, as in かかない and きかない。
texts.The ta form changes ku to ita. So kaku b: The た form changes く to いた. So かく becomes かいた, きく becomes きいた, and はたらく becomes はたらいた. The past negative is かかなかった.
texts.There is one important exception. The ve: There is one important exception. The verb いく (go) ends in く, but the book does not put it in this group. It is starred and listed in Group 5, because its た form is いった, not いいた. Its ない form is ordinary, いかない, and its past negative is いかなかった.
texts.10.7 Group 5: verbs that end in u, tsu o: 10.7 Group 5: verbs that end in う, つ or る (page 149)
texts.Group 5 is the biggest group. It has the: Group 5 is the biggest group. It has the verbs that end in う (かう, うたう, すう), in つ (まつ, もつ) and in る (わかる, うる, つくる, はじまる, おわる, はいる). Three different endings, but one shared result: the た form of all of them ends in った.
texts.For the ta form, u, tsu and ru all becom: For the た form, う, つ and る all become った. So かう becomes かった, まつ becomes まった, and わかる becomes わかった. For the ない form, the last sound changes to the a row, but there are two things to watch. A verb that ends in う takes わ, not a, so かう becomes かわない and すう becomes すわない. A verb that ends in つ takes た, so まつ becomes またない. A verb that ends in る takes ら, so わかる becomes わからない.
texts.Two verbs in this group are starred in t: Two verbs in this group are starred in the book because they look like something else. The verb いく (go) is listed here because its た form is いった, like the others. The verb かえる (go home) ends in える, which makes it look Regular, but it follows the Group 5 rules, so it is かえらない and かえった. The book's footnote adds しる (know), はいる (enter), はしる (run) and きる (cut) to the same list. These verbs all end in える or いる but belong to Group 5, so they are しらない, はいらない, はしらない and きらない, and しった, はいった, はしった and きった。
texts.10.8 Regular verbs: eru and iru (page 14: 10.8 Regular verbs: える and いる (page 149)
texts.Regular verbs end in eru or iru in the d: Regular verbs end in える or いる in the dictionary form, and they are the easiest to change. To make the ない form, drop る and add ない. To make the た form, drop る and add た. For the past negative, drop る and add なかった. For example, たべる becomes たべない, たべた and たべなかった, and みる becomes みない, みた and みなかった。
texts.There is no change in the last sound, so: There is no change in the last sound, so you never have to think about んだ, った or いた. The only trouble is knowing which verbs are Regular. The rule is that a verb that ends in える or いる is Regular, with the exceptions in Group 5: かえる, しる, はいる, はしる and きる. The verb おきる (wake up) ends in いる and is Regular, so it is おきない and おきた。
texts.10.9 Special verbs: suru and kuru (page: 10.9 Special verbs: する and くる (page 149)
texts.The two Special verbs are suru (do) and: The two Special verbs are する (do) and くる (come), and their forms are fixed, so you simply memorize them. The forms of する are する, しない, した and しなかった. The forms of くる are くる, こない, きた and こなかった。
texts.Every noun + suru verb follows suru. So: Every noun + する verb follows する. So べんきょうする becomes べんきょうしない, べんきょうした and べんきょうしなかった. In the same way, テニスする becomes テニスした.
texts.Watch the first sound of kuru. In the di: Watch the first sound of くる. In the dictionary form and the た form it is く and き, but in the ない form and the なかった form it is こ, as in こない and こなかった。
texts.10.10 Masu form to the dictionary form:: 10.10 ます form to the dictionary form: present positive (page 151)
texts.The first conversion is from masu to the: The first conversion is from ます to the dictionary form, the informal present positive. You already know how to do this from Chapter 9. Remove ます to get the stem, and then follow the rules for the verb type. For example, かいものします becomes かいものする, たべます becomes たべる, よみます becomes よむ, and やすみます becomes やすむ.
texts.The dictionary form is also the casual w: The dictionary form is also the casual way to talk about the future. The sentence あした かいものする means I will go shopping tomorrow. The same form covers habits, as in まいあさ よむ (I read every morning).
texts.In the book's examples some markers are: In the book's examples some markers are put in brackets, such as (に) and (を). That means they are often dropped in casual talk. Lesson 10.16 explains this.
texts.10.11 Masen to the nai form: present neg: 10.11 ません to the ない form: present negative (page 151)
texts.To make the informal present negative, c: To make the informal present negative, change the verb to its ない form. The rule depends on the group. For Group 1 to Group 5, the final う sound changes to the a sound and ない is added (のむ becomes のまない, かう becomes かわない). For Regular verbs, drop る and add ない (たべる becomes たべない). For Special verbs, する becomes しない and くる becomes こない.
texts.The book gives two notes about markers i: The book gives two notes about markers in negative sentences. The first is that を sometimes changes into は when the sentence turns negative, as in コーヒー は のまない. The second is that は can be added after に and へ in a negative sentence for more emphasis, as in ごじ には おわらない (it does not end at five, though).
texts.Remember that the nai form is the casual: Remember that the ない form is the casual twin of ません. It does not mean past tense.
texts.10.12 Mashita to the ta form: past posit: 10.12 ました to the た form: past positive (page 152)
texts.The ta form is the informal past positiv: The た form is the informal past positive. For Regular verbs, drop る and add た (おきる becomes おきた). For Special verbs, する becomes した and くる becomes きた. For the five Irregular groups, the ending depends on the last sound of the dictionary form:
texts.bu, mu and nu become nda (yasumu becomes: ぶ, む and ぬ become んだ (やすむ becomes やすんだ).
ぐ becomes いだ (およぐ becomes およいだ).
texts.su becomes shita (hanasu becomes hanashi: す becomes した (はなす becomes はなした).
texts.ku becomes ita (kaku becomes kaita), exc: く becomes いた (かく becomes かいた), except いく, which becomes いった.
texts.u, tsu and ru become tta (kau becomes ka: う, つ and る become った (かう becomes かった, まつ becomes まった, かえる becomes かえった).
texts.10.13 Masen deshita to the nakatta form:: 10.13 ません でした to the なかった form: past negative (page 152)
texts.The nakatta form is the informal past ne: The なかった form is the informal past negative. To make it, take the ない form and replace the final い with かった. So よまない becomes よまなかった, たべない becomes たべなかった, and こない becomes こなかった.
texts.This works exactly like the past tense o: This works exactly like the past tense of an い-adjective, because ない itself behaves like an い-adjective. The word ない ends in い, and the past of ない is なかった, in the same way that たかい (expensive) becomes たかかった (was expensive).
texts.Do not mix up the nai form and the nakat: Do not mix up the ない form and the なかった form. The form たべない means I do not eat, and たべなかった means I did not eat.
texts.The first set on this page changes a pre: The first set on this page changes a present sentence into a past sentence. The change happens in the verb only. Every other part of the sentence stays the same. Each row below shows the present sentence first and the past sentence after the slash. Notice that a negative present (そうじしない) turns into a negative past (そうじしなかった).
texts.The second set changes a positive senten: The second set changes a positive sentence into a negative one. Use the ない form for a present sentence and the なかった form for a past sentence. The tense does not change. For example, へんじした (past) becomes へんじしなかった (past), and のむ (present) becomes のまない (present). Each row below shows the positive sentence first and the negative sentence after the slash.
texts.In casual speech and writing, the marker: In casual speech and writing, the markers を, が, に and へ are sometimes left out. Say コーヒー のむ instead of コーヒー を のむ, and にほん いく instead of にほん へ いく. The meaning does not change, because the listener can work out the job of the word from the situation.
texts.The other markers are not dropped. The m: The other markers are not dropped. The markers で (by, at), と (with), から (from) and まで (until) all carry meaning that the listener cannot guess, so they stay.
texts.In negative sentences you may see two sm: In negative sentences you may see two small changes. The marker を can turn into は, and は can be added after へ and に for extra emphasis. These changes are optional, and they are never required.
texts.10.17 Ending markers no and wa with each: 10.17 Ending markers の and わ with each word type (page 155)
texts.Two ending markers are introduced in thi: Two ending markers are introduced in this chapter: no, which asks a casual question, and わ, a soft ending for a woman. Which form you attach them to depends on the word before them.
texts.An informal verb takes no or wa directly: An informal verb takes の or わ directly: いく の, いく わ。
texts.An i-adjective takes no or wa directly:: An い-adjective takes の or わ directly: たかい の, たかい わ。
texts.A na-adjective takes nano or dawa: kirei: A な-adjective takes なの or だわ: きれい なの, きれい だわ。
texts.A noun takes nano or dawa: igirisujin na: A noun takes なの or だわ: イギリスじん なの, イギリスじん だわ。
texts.In other words, the na-adjectives and no: In other words, the な-adjectives and nouns need an extra な or だ. You can think of it this way: です becomes だ, and だ turns into な in front of の. Each row below shows the question with の first and the statement with は after the slash.
texts.10.18 Casual questions with no (bunkei 1: 10.18 Casual questions with no (ぶんけい 10.2, page 155)
texts.In casual speech, the question marker ka: In casual speech, the question marker か is replaced by の. The question いきます か becomes いく の, and おわりました か becomes おわった の. The verb is in the informal form, and your voice goes up at the end of the sentence. In writing, a question mark shows that it is a question.
texts.When a question word is used, no goes at: When a question word is used, no goes at the end in the same way. Questions such as どこへ いくの (where are you going) and なにを たべたの (what did you eat) are everyday casual questions. A question with only a question word, such as いつ (when), can stand alone.
texts.Some of the book's casual questions, suc: Some of the book's casual questions, such as かいぎ おわったの, end in a full stop, but they are still questions. The no marker is also used by both men and women. The soft は in the next lesson is the one that is used mostly by women.
texts.10.19 Ending marker wa for women (bunkei: 10.19 Ending marker わ for women (ぶんけい 10.3, page 155)
texts.The ending wa is a soft ending that wome: The ending わ is a soft ending that women often use to give an opinion, to make something clearer or to show a feeling. It goes at the end of a casual sentence. The book calls it an ending marker for a female speaker.
texts.After a verb or an i-adjective, you add: After a verb or an い-adjective, you add は directly: いく は, おいしかったわ. After a noun or a な-adjective, you add だ first, so きれいです becomes きれいだ は and イギリスじんです becomes イギリスじんだわ. Remember that です and ます are dropped, because the sentence is casual.
texts.Be careful with the spelling. This endin: Be careful with the spelling. This ending is written わ in hiragana, and it is not the topic marker は, which is written は. They sound the same, but they have different jobs. In the same sentence, you can see both, as in ふじさんは きれいだわ (Mount Fuji is beautiful).
texts.The book shows the same conversation bet: The book shows the same conversation between Ben and Mari twice. The first half is formal, and the second half is informal. Compare them line by line. Every ます turns into the dictionary form, です disappears, か turns into no or just a rising voice, and だ appears in front of よ (だいじょうぶ だ よ). The short endings ね and よ stay.
texts.In the informal half, the sentence that: In the informal half, the sentence that ends in です か, such as いつですか, loses everything and becomes いつ. The question mark in the informal half is added to the book's text so that the questions are easy to spot. Also notice that Ben still says はい in the book's informal version, even though a friend would often say something shorter.
texts.10.21 Informal desu and informal adjecti: 10.21 Informal です and informal adjectives (extra lesson)
texts.This extra lesson fills a gap in the cha: This extra lesson fills a gap in the chapter. The book uses informal です and informal adjectives in its examples (きれいだ は, おいしかったわ), but it never gives you the full set.
texts.For nouns and na-adjectives, desu become: For nouns and な-adjectives, です becomes だ, じゃ ありません becomes じゃない, でした becomes だった, and じゃ ありません でした becomes じゃなかった. For い-adjectives, you simply drop です: たかいです becomes たかい, たかくないです becomes たかくない, and たかかったです becomes たかかった.
texts.The adjective ii (good) is still the exc: The adjective いい (good) is still the exception. It uses its other form よい for the negative and the past, so you get よくない and よかった. Never say いいくない or いいかった。
texts.This table pulls together the verbs from: This table pulls together the verbs from Chapters 7 to 10. Each row shows the dictionary form, the ない form, the た form and the なかった form, followed by the verb's type. It is a good list to memorize, because the informal forms are where most mistakes happen.
texts.The last two rows are extras that the bo: The last two rows are extras that the book does not cover in this chapter. The verb ある (exist) is unusual, because its negative is the word ない itself, not あらない. The verb いる (be present, for people and animals) is a Regular verb, so it is いない and いた。

texts.The reading exercises at the end of the: The reading exercises at the end of the chapter include a trip to さっぽろ and a letter from Ana to John. Many of their sentences are useful on their own. This table lists the key sentences so that you can read the passages with confidence and reuse the phrases. All the sentences in these passages are formal. Try changing each one to the informal form as extra practice.
texts.Notice that the letter uses ordinary for: Notice that the letter uses ordinary formal verbs in the past (みました, かえりました) and the present (ざんぎょうします), which is the normal style for a letter と a friend you do not speak to every day.
さっぽろ is in the north of Japan.
In さっぽろ I saw many kinds of places.
texts.The new verbs in this chapter each have: The new verbs in this chapter each have a few nouns they like to go with, and learning them in pairs makes the sentences come quicker. Most take their noun with を. Two are different: わかる takes what you understand with が, as in 日本語が わかる, and しる is mostly used in the negative, as in アナさんを しらない (I don't know Ana).
texts.Dasu also goes with tegami (a letter), t: だす also goes with てがみ (a letter), つかう with けいたい and パソコン, つくる with ごはん, まつ with a vehicle such as バス, もつ with にもつ (luggage), and おぼえる with かんじ.

texts.asobimasu means to play or to have fun,: あそびます means to play or to have fun, as in ともだち to あそびます. It is not used for a sport.

texts.Regular look-alikes such as miru, okiru: Regular look-alikes such as みる, おきる and たべる really are Regular.
texts.Kiita, kita and kitta: きいた, きた and きった
texts.kiita comes from kiku and means listened: きいた comes from きく and means listened or asked.

texts.The sounds are close, so listen for the: The sounds are close, so listen for the small つ and for the long いい.
texts.Itta, hanashita and shita: いった, はなした and した
いった is the た form of いく, went.
texts.hanashita is the ta form of hanasu, spok: はなした is the た form of はなす, spoke. It ends in した, but the verb is not する.
texts.shita on its own is the ta form of suru,: した on its own is the た form of する, did.
texts.Nai or nakatta: ない or なかった
texts.nai is the present negative. tabenai mea: ない is the present negative. たべない means I do not eat.
texts.nakatta is the past negative. tabenakatt: なかった is the past negative. たべなかった means I did not eat.
texts.To go from nai to nakatta, change the la: To go from ない to なかった, change the last い to かった.
texts.Do not use nai for something that alread: Do not use ない for something that already happened.
よんだ can be よむ (read) or よぶ (call). のんだ is のむ. あそんだ is あそぶ. やすんだ is やすむ. しんだ is しぬ.
texts.All of them end in nda. The sentence tel: All of them end in んだ. The sentence tells you which verb is meant.
texts.katta is kau (buy). Do not mix it up wit: かった is かう (buy). Do not mix it up with the た form of an い-adjective, such as たかかった (was expensive).
texts.iku can mean I go or I will go. The time: いく can mean I go or I will go. The time word tells you which one. あした いく is I will go tomorrow.
texts.A past time word needs the ta form: kino: A past time word needs the た form: きのう いった。
texts.With ka the verb must be in the masu for: With か the verb must be in the ます form: いきます か。

texts.The one at the end is always after an in: The one at the end is always after an informal verb, an い-adjective, or なの after a noun or な-adjective。

texts.de, to, kara and made are not dropped, b: で, と, から and まで are not dropped, because they carry meaning that cannot be guessed.
texts.In negative sentences o can change to wa: In negative sentences を can change to は, and は can be added after に and へ. These are optional.

texts.Are you not coming to tomorrow's party?: Are you not coming to tomorrow's party? The place comes first, then へ, then the ない form, and no at the end makes it a casual question. The book prints a full stop here, but no after a verb marks a question.
texts.4 2 1 3: yamada san wa maishuu kinyoubi: 4 2 1 3: やまださんは まいしゅう きんようびに へやを そうじする。
texts.Yamada cleans the room on Fridays every: Yamada cleans the room on Fridays every week. A day of the week takes に, and へや takes を. The verb そうじする is already printed.
texts.2 1 4 3: kinou no yoru taijin no tomodac: 2 1 4 3: きのうの よる タイじんの ともだちと はなびを みた。
texts.Last night I watched fireworks with a Th: Last night I watched fireworks with a Thai friend. The time comes first, then タイじん の ともだち to for the companion, then はなび. The を is printed after the blanks.
texts.3 2 4 1: imouto wa maiasa zenzen hayaku: 3 2 4 1: いもうとは まいあさ ぜんぜん はやく おきない。
texts.My younger sister never gets up early in: My younger sister never gets up early in the morning. The time word comes first, and ぜんぜん sits right before はやく and the negative verb おきない. If your key puts はやく before ぜんぜん, that is only a small difference in word order.
texts.4 1 3 2: otousan wa osake to ko-ra o ama: 4 1 3 2: おとうさんは おさけとコーラを あまり のまない。
texts.My father does not drink alcohol and col: My father does not drink alcohol and cola much. おさけ to コーラ is the thing, を marks it, and あまり goes with the negative verb のまない.
texts.3 1 4 2: watashi wa kinou kouen no mae d: 3 1 4 2: わたしは きのう こうえんの まえで まった。
I waited in front of the park yesterday. こうえん の まえ means in front of the park, and で marks where the waiting happened.
texts.2 4 1 3: kyonen kim san to nihongo o nih: 2 4 1 3: きょねん キムさんと にほんごを にほんで べんきょうした。
texts.Last year I studied Japanese in Japan wi: Last year I studied Japanese in Japan with Kim. と marks the companion, にほんご を is what was studied, and にほん で is the place. The で is printed after the blanks.
texts.The passage is a trip to Sapporo last Fe: The passage is a trip to さっぽろ last February with the family. It was cold and pretty, and the writer enjoyed the snow festival, a hot spring and skiing.
ふゆ の きせつ means the winter season. The other choices are a photo, a game and laundry, and none of them fits after ふゆ の.
texts.The writer went with father, mother, an: The writer went with father, mother, an older sister and an older brother. Counting the writer, that is five people, so ごにん で. If you count only the four relatives, you get よにん, but the writer is travelling too.
texts.The trip happened last year, and the sen: The trip happened last year, and the sentence before it is past (でした), so use the past positive たのしかった. とてもたのしかったです means it was very fun.
texts.The letter says senshuu no nichiyoubi ni: The letter says せんしゅうの にちようびに かいしゃの ともだちと こうえんで はなみを みました. Ana went to a park to see the cherry blossoms with friends from work.
texts.4 hitori de kaerimasu (ひとりで かえります): 4 ひとりで かえります
texts.The letter only says juugonichi ni firip: The letter only says じゅうごにちに フィリピンへ かえります, and it names nobody to go with. Jon is the person she writes to, the friends from work were at the park, and the family trip was Jon's, so the only choice left is ひとりで (alone).
texts.These ask about you, so the answers belo: These ask about you, so the answers below are samples. Each one shows the pattern the question is drilling. Any true answer in a casual sentence works. A negative answer also works, for example いいえ, しない.
texts.kuji kara goji made shigotosuru. (くじから ご: くじから ごじまで しごとする。
texts.nanji kara nanji made asks for a start t: なんじ から なんじ まで asks for a start time and an end time. Choose べんきょうする or しごとする. Sample meaning: I work from nine to five.
texts.hai, mainichi benkyousuru. isshuukan ni: はい、まいにち べんきょうする。いっしゅうかんに ごじかん べんきょうする。
texts.The first question is a yes or no questi: The first question is a yes or no question, so start with はい or いいえ. なんじかん asks how many hours. Sample meaning: Yes, I study every day. I study five hours a week.
texts.ichinichi ni sanjikan gurai keitai o tsu: いちにちに さんじかんぐらい けいたいを つかう。
texts.dono gurai asks how long. Answer with an: どの ぐらい asks how long. Answer with an amount of time and つかう. Sample meaning: I use my cell phone for about three hours a day.
texts.hai, taberu. resutoran de taberu. (はい、たべ: はい、たべる。レストランで たべる。
texts.The first question is yes or no. doko de: The first question is yes or no. どこで asks where, so answer with a place and で. Sample meaning: Yes, I do. I eat at a restaurant.
texts.nan no supo-tsu asks which sport. A spor: なん の スポーツ asks which sport. A sport takes する, so テニスする. Sample meaning: Yes, I do. I play tennis.
texts.hai, mita. nihon no eiga o mita. (はい、みた。: はい、みた。にほんの えいがを みた。
texts.The question is in the past, so use mita: The question is in the past, so use みた. なにを asks what. Sample meaning: Yes, I did. I watched a Japanese movie.
texts.hai, maishuu soujisuru. (はい、まいしゅう そうじする。: はい、まいしゅう そうじする。
texts.This is a yes or no question about a hab: This is a yes or no question about a habit, so answer with はい or いいえ and the dictionary form. Sample meaning: Yes, I clean every week.
texts.kazoku to nihon e iku. (かぞくと にほんへ いく。): かぞくと にほんへ いく。
texts.doko asks where, so name a place. The ma: どこ asks where, so name a place. The marker へ is kept here, and it can also be dropped. Sample meaning: I will go to Japan with my family.
texts.hai, itta. mo-ru de kaimonoshita. (はい、いっ: はい、いった。モールで かいものした。
texts.The first question is past and yes or no: The first question is past and yes or no, so answer with いった. なにを asks what you did. Sample meaning: Yes, I went. I went shopping at the mall.
texts.doko e asks where to, so answer with a p: どこへ asks where to, so answer with a place and へ. Sample meaning: I will go to the park.
texts.These answers are casual, to match the c: These answers are casual, to match the chapter. The formal ます style is also correct. Word order can shift a little in all of them, as long as the verb stays last.
texts.konban tomodachi to dekakeru. (こんばん ともだち: こんばん ともだちと でかける。
texts.dekakeru means go out. It is a Regular v: でかける means go out. It is a Regular verb, and the dictionary form covers the future. と marks the companion, and こんばん takes no に.
texts.ashita sensei ni soudansuru. (あした せんせいに: あした せんせいに そうだんする。
texts.soudansuru takes ni for the person you c: そうだんする takes に for the person you consult. あした takes no に.
texts.kurasume-to ni setsumeisuru. (クラスメートに せつ: クラスメートに せつめいする。
texts.setsumeisuru takes ni for the person you: せつめいする takes に for the person you explain to. クラスメート is a classmate, with a hyphen for the long vowel.
texts.mainichi gakkou de renshuusuru. (まいにち がっ: まいにち がっこうで れんしゅうする。
texts.de marks the place of the action. mainic: で marks the place of the action. まいにち takes no に. れんしゅうする means practice.
texts.kinou rokujikan kuruma o untenshita. (きの: きのう ろくじかん くるまを うんてんした。
texts.kuruma o untensuru means drive a car, an: くるま を うんてんする means drive a car, and the past is うんてんした. ろくじかん is a length of time, and it takes no particle.
texts.konshuu no nichiyoubi ni tomodachi to go: こんしゅうの にちようびに ともだちと ゴルフする。
texts.ni marks the day of the week. A sport ta: に marks the day of the week. A sport takes する, so golf is ゴルフする.
texts.isshuukan ni ichido heya o soujisuru. (い: いっしゅうかんに いちど へやを そうじする。
texts.isshuukan ni ichido means once a week. h: いっしゅうかん に いちど means once a week. へや を そうじする is clean the room.
texts.maishuu getsuyoubi ni joushi ni repo-to: まいしゅう げつようびに じょうしに レポートを だす。
texts.joushi is a supervisor, and ni marks the: じょうし is a supervisor, and に marks the person you hand the report to. だす means submit.
texts.tenisu wa shinai. / tenisushinai. (テニスは: テニスは しない。 / テニスしない。
texts.A sport takes suru, so the negative is s: A sport takes する, so the negative is しない. In a negative sentence を can change to は for emphasis, and テニスしない also works.
texts.konban hitori de hanabi o miru. (こんばん ひと: こんばん ひとりで はなびを みる。
texts.hitori de means alone. hanabi o miru is: ひとりで means alone. はなび を みる is watch fireworks, and the dictionary form covers the future.

texts.These five sounds are the base of every: These five sounds are the base of every other row, so learn them first. Each vowel is short and clean. Say あ as in father, い as in see, う as in food (with relaxed lips), え as in pet and お as in more, but shorter. Keep your mouth still while you say each one, so it does not glide into a second sound as in English.
texts.Katakana uses the same five vowel sounds: Katakana uses the same five vowel sounds as hiragana: ア as in father, イ as in see, ウ as in food (with relaxed lips), エ as in pet and オ as in more, but shorter. Only the shapes are new. Katakana strokes are short, straight and angular, and many of them are parts of kanji.

texts.One spelling breaks the pattern: し is sh: One spelling breaks the pattern: し is し, not si. It sounds like the English word シェ. The う in す is often very quiet at the end of a word, as in です, which you meet in the silent vowels lesson.
texts.One spelling breaks the pattern: シ is sh: One spelling breaks the pattern: シ is し, not si, and it sounds like the English word シェ. Be careful, because シ looks a lot like ツ and ソ looks a lot like ン. The Easy to mix up section shows how to tell them apart.

texts.Two sounds break the pattern: ち is chi a: Two sounds break the pattern: ち is ち and つ is つ. For つ, put the tip of your tongue just behind your top teeth, say the ts at the end of the English word cats, then add う. Do not say tu or す。
texts.Memory hooks: た is the letters t and a s: Memory hooks: た is the letters t and a squeezed together. ち looks like a 5, so picture five slices of cheese. つ is a tsunami wave curling over. て is an open hand, and the kanji for hand, 手, is read て. と is a toe with a thorn stuck in it.

texts.This is an n sound in front of each vowe: This is an ん sound in front of each vowel. Do not mix the whole row up with ん, the single n kana at the end of the chart. Two characters here, ぬ and ね, are easy to confuse with め and れ, so read the Easy to mix up section when you are ready.
texts.Memory hooks: な is a nun kneeling in pra: Memory hooks: な is a nun kneeling in prayer. に looks like 二, the number two, which is read に. ぬ is a noodle wound around a chopstick. ね is a cat (ねこ) with a curled tail. の is a circle with a swish, like a sign saying no.
Memory hooks: ナ is just the nun's cross. ニ is two lines, like the kanji 二, which is read に. ヌ is a noodle pinched into a sharp bend. ネ is the knot of a necktie, and it starts ネクタイ. ノ is a single slash, like the line through a no-entry sign.

texts.ふ is fu, made by blowing softly between: ふ is ふ, made by blowing softly between your lips, somewhere between English f and h. は and へ change their sound when they work as grammar words: は is read わ and へ is read え. You practise that in the particles lesson.
texts.Memory hooks: は is a person laughing out: Memory hooks: は is a person laughing out loud, は は. ひ is a wide grin, へえ へえ. ふ is Mount Fuji with a patch of cloud. へ is a hill: hey, a hill! ほ is は with an extra bar, like Santa laughing ほ ほ ほ.
texts.フ is fu, made by blowing softly between: フ is ふ, made by blowing softly between your lips, somewhere between English f and h. Katakana has no particles, so ハ and ヘ always keep the sounds は and へ.
texts.M row (ma mi mu me mo): M row (ま み む め も)
texts.Memory hooks: ま is a mama with her arms: Memory hooks: ま is a mama with her arms out and a bundle at her feet. み is a number 3 with a tail, and みっつ means three. む is a cow saying moo, with a small horn on the right. め is an eye, and the kanji for eye, 目, is read me. も is a fish hook with two worms, and you want も(れ) worms.
texts.Memory hooks: マ is a mallet with a flat: Memory hooks: マ is a mallet with a flat head and a slanted handle. ミ is three slanted lines, like the number 3, and みっつ means three. ム is the cow's pointed snout and horn. メ is an X, and X marks me. モ is a fish hook straightened out, with two worms.

texts.Memory hooks: ヤ is a yacht with a tall m: Memory hooks: ヤ is a yacht with a tall mast and a slanted sail. ユ is a U-shaped pool, and ゆ means hot water. ヨ is a backwards E with three bars.

texts.わ is wa. を is pronounced o, exactly like: わ is は. を is pronounced お, exactly like お. In modern Japanese you use it only as a particle that marks what a verb acts on, so you will almost never see it inside a word. In romaji it is written を, though some systems write を.
texts.Memory hooks: わ is someone shouting wa!: Memory hooks: わ is someone shouting は! in surprise. を is an acrobat in mid-air shouting woah.
texts.ワ is wa. ヲ is pronounced o, like オ, but: ワ is the katakana partner of わ. ヲ has the same sound as オ, but it is very rare because katakana has no particle that needs it. You will find it mostly in the spelling ヲタク and in old or stylized writing. Spend your time on ワ.

texts.ん is the only kana that is a consonant w: ん is the only kana that is a consonant with no vowel. It is a full beat on its own, so こんにちは has five beats: こ, n, に, ち, は. No word begins with ん. You always write ん, but your mouth changes a little around it: before b, m or p it sounds like m, and before k or g it sounds like ng, which your Chapter 1 phonetics page shows with しんぶん and てんき。
texts.When ん comes before a vowel or a y sound: When ん comes before a vowel or a y sound, romaji adds an apostrophe so you can see the break. Compare きん'えん (no smoking) with きねん (anniversary).

texts.Two small dashes, called dakuten (or ten: Two small dashes, called だくてん (or 点々), turn a k sound into a g sound. The mouth shape stays the same, but your throat hums. Put your fingers on your throat to feel it. Some speakers soften g to ng in the middle of a word, so ありがとう can sound like ありんがとう. Both are fine.
texts.The dakuten is only a mark. If you can r: The だくてん is only a mark. If you can read か, you can already read が.
texts.Two small dashes, called dakuten (or ten: Two small dashes, called だくてん (or 点々), turn a k sound into a g sound. They work exactly as in hiragana: say the plain sound, hum it, and you have the marked one.

texts.Dakuten on the s row gives the z row. ジ: Two small marks on the さ row produce ざ、じ、ず、ぜ and ぞ. In katakana the corresponding characters are ザ、ジ、ズ、ゼ and ゾ. Practise ジ in ジープ and ジュース. Reveal romaji to compare the spelling notes.

texts.Dakuten on the t row gives だ, で and ど, w: だくてん on the t row gives だ, で and ど, which are regular. ぢ and づ also exist, but they sound exactly like じ and ず, and they appear in only a few words, usually when ち or つ becomes voiced inside a word. When you write じ or ず yourself, use じ and ず.
texts.Dakuten on the t row gives ダ, デ and ド, w: だくてん on the t row gives ダ, デ and ド, which are regular. ヂ and ヅ also exist, but they sound exactly like ジ and ズ, and they are almost never used in katakana, so they have no katakana example word here. When you write じ or ず, use ジ and ズ.

texts.A small circle, called handakuten, turns: A small circle, called はんだくてん, turns an h sound into a p sound. It is used only on the h row, so there are exactly five of these kana. Be careful: two dashes make b and a small circle makes p, so は becomes ば or ぱ.

texts.A combination sound, which your Chapter: A combination sound, which your Chapter 1 phonetics page calls a contracted sound, joins a kana that ends in い with a small や, ゆ or よ. The two kana make one beat. Write the small kana smaller, low on the line and close to the kana before it. So きゃ is きゃ, one beat, while き followed by a full-size や is き・や, two beats.
texts.The pattern is easy: take the i kana, dr: The pattern is easy: take the い kana, drop the い, and add や, ゆ or よ。 き (き) becomes きゃ, きゅ and きょ。

texts.Here the h, b and p rows blend with a sm: Here the h, b and p rows blend with a small や, ゆ or よ. You will see ひゃく (100) and びょうき (illness) most often. These combinations also show up in number words: さんびゃく (300) uses びゃ, and はっぴゃく (800) uses a small っ and ぴゃ。
texts.The h, b and p rows blend with a small ユ: The h, b and p rows blend with a small ユ or ヨ in a handful of loanwords. The combinations ヒャ (ひゃ), ビャ (びゃ) and ピャ (ぴゃ) exist too, but they are so rare in katakana that they have no katakana example word here.

texts.The same rule works for m and r: み plus: The same rule works for m and r: み plus a small や is みゃ, and り plus a small よ is りょ. The most useful ones are りょ, りゅ and みょ. The kana みゅ (みゅ) exists but no everyday word uses it.
texts.The same rule works for m and r: ミ plus: The same rule works for m and r: ミ plus a small ヤ is みゃ, and リ plus a small ユ is りゅ. Words like ミュージック (music) and リュック (backpack) are the ones you will meet most often.
texts.A small っ makes no sound of its own. It: A small ッ marks a short pause that doubles the next consonant. Examples are サッカー、ベッド、カップ and キッチン. A small ッ usually sits in the middle of a word and counts as one full beat. Reveal romaji to compare the spelling rule.
texts.A small ッ makes no sound of its own. It: A small ッ marks a short pause that doubles the next consonant. Examples are サッカー、ベッド、カップ and キッチン. A small ッ usually sits in the middle of a word and counts as one full beat. Reveal romaji to compare the spelling rule.
texts.A long vowel lasts twice as long as a sh: A long vowel lasts twice as long as a short one, and the length can change the word. In hiragana, add あ to an あ sound, い to an い sound, う to an う sound, え to an え sound, or お to an お sound.
texts.Two spellings need special care. A long: Two spellings need special care. Some long え sounds are written with え, as in おねえさん, but most use い, as in せんせい. A long お is usually written with う, as in こうこう, but a few words use お, as in おおきい. Reveal romaji to compare these spellings.
texts.Katakana does not add a vowel kana to ma: Katakana does not add a vowel kana to make a long vowel. It uses a dash called ー instead, which means hold the vowel before it for twice as long. In romaji it is written as a hyphen, so コーヒー is コーヒー. In horizontal text the dash lies flat, and in vertical text it stands upright.
texts.The dash matters, because length changes: The dash matters, because length changes the word: ビル (ビル) is a building and ビール (ビール) is beer.
texts.Particles は, へ and を (wa, e, o): Particles は, へ and を
texts.Three hiragana change their sound when t: Three hiragana change their sound when they work as particles, the small grammar words that attach to other words. は is read わ、へ is read え and を is read お. In other words they keep their usual sounds, as in はる and へや. Reveal romaji to compare these readings.
texts.The greetings こんにちは and こんばんは end in は r: The greetings こんにちは and こんばんは end in は read わ for the same historical reason.

texts.Katakana has extra combinations for soun: Katakana has extra combinations for sounds that native Japanese words do not have. A small vowel (ァ ィ ェ ォ) after a full-size kana blends with it into one beat. The big kana gives the consonant and the small vowel gives the vowel. フ plus a small ア is ファ.

texts.テ plus a small ィ is ti, and デ plus a sma: テ plus a small ィ is ティ, and デ plus a small ィ is ディ. Native Japanese words have no ティ or ディ, so these combinations were added for foreign words. Two rarer sounds follow the same rule: トゥ is tu and ドゥ is どぅ.
Read ティ as one beat. It is not て・い.

texts.ウ plus a small ィ, ェ or ォ gives wi, we an: ウ plus a small ィ, ェ or ォ gives ウィ, we and を. Note that ウォーター is ウォーター, not うおーたー, because the small kana blends with ウ into one beat.

texts.ヴ is ウ with two dots, and it stands for: ヴ is ウ with two dots, and it stands for the English v. With a small ァ, ィ, ェ or ォ it gives ヴァ, ヴィ, ヴェ and ヴォ. Many words use バ, ビ, ブ, ベ and ボ instead, so you may see both spellings, such as ヴァイオリン and バイオリン for violin. The plain ヴ (vu) is rare.

texts.When you write ji or zu yourself, use じ: When you write じ or ず yourself, use じ and ず. ぢ and づ appear in only a few words, such as はなぢ (はなぢ, nosebleed) and つづく (つづく, to continue).

texts.を is used only as a particle that marks: を is used only as a particle that marks what a verb acts on, as in ほんを よみます (ほん を よみます, I read a book).

texts.Inside a word they keep their normal sou: Inside a word they keep their normal sounds: はる is はる and へや is へや.
texts.The greetings こんにちは (konnichiwa) and こんば: The greetings こんにちは (こんにちは) and こんばんは (こんばんは) end in は read わ.
texts.A full-size つ says tsu. A small っ is a p: A full-size つ says つ. A small っ is a pause that doubles the next sound: きつね (きつね, fox) has a full-size つ, and きって (きって, postal stamp) has a small っ.
texts.びょういん (byouin, hospital) and びよういん (biyo: びょういん (びょういん, hospital) and びよういん (びよういん, beauty salon) differ only in the size of one kana.

texts.ん is its own beat, so きんえん (kin'en, no s: ん is its own beat, so きんえん (きん'えん, no smoking) has four beats and きねん (きねん, anniversary) has three.
texts.Romaji shows the break with an apostroph: Romaji shows the break with an apostrophe: きん'えん and ほんや (ほんや, bookstore).
texts.Without the apostrophe, kin'en would loo: Without the apostrophe, きん'えん would look just like きねん, which is a different word.
texts.When a shape is unclear, look at the wor: When a shape is unclear, look at the words around it. A word まで of other hiragana is hiragana, and a foreign word like コーヒー is katakana.

texts.Two small dashes (dakuten) make a voiced: Two small dashes (だくてん) make a voiced sound, so ハ (は) becomes バ (ば) and ヘ becomes ベ.

texts.ヂ sounds exactly like ジ, and ヅ sounds ex: ヂ sounds exactly like ジ, and ヅ sounds exactly like ズ. Romaji spells them じ and ず。
They are almost never used in katakana. When you write じ or ず yourself, use ジ and ズ.
texts.Both are read o. ヲ is very rare, and you: Both are read を. ヲ is very rare, and you will mostly see it in the spelling ヲタク (おたく).
texts.When you write o in katakana, use オ, as: When you write を in katakana, use オ, as in オフィス (オフィス, office).
texts.A full-size ツ says tsu. A small ッ is a p: A full-size ツ says つ. A small ッ is a pause that doubles the next sound: ツアー (ツアー, tour) has a full-size ツ, and カップ (カップ, cup) has a small ッ.
texts.一 is the kanji for one (ichi). It looks: 一 is the kanji for one (いち). It looks like ー but it is a different character, so use the surrounding text to decide.
texts.A small vowel after a full-size kana ble: A small vowel after a full-size kana blends into one beat. ティ is ティ, with one beat.
texts.A full-size イ after テ makes two beats. テ: A full-size イ after テ makes two beats. テイ would be て・い.
texts.So パーティー (pa-ti-, party) uses a small ィ,: So パーティー (パーティー, party) uses a small ィ, and it has four beats, not five.

texts.Most kanji have two kinds of reading. Th: Most kanji have two kinds of reading. The workbook calls them the Japanese reading (訓読み) and the Chinese reading (音読み), and the tables on this page list them as 訓読み and 音読み.

texts.The same two kinds of reading from Kanji: The same two kinds of reading from Kanji 1 apply here. The Japanese reading (訓読み) is meaning-based and usually appears when a kanji stands alone or has kana after it. The Chinese reading (音読み) is sound-based and usually appears inside compound words. As in Kanji 1, the tables write the Chinese reading in katakana.

texts.After hajimemashite, the set phrase is d: After はじめまして, the set phrase is どうぞ よろしく おねがいします. It is what you say when you meet someone for the first time.
texts.no links two nouns and shows who or what: no links two nouns and shows who or what something belongs to. さくら かいしゃ の しゃちょう means the president of さくら company.
texts.doko asks where. dare is who, dore is wh: どこ asks where. だれ is who, どれ is which one and いつ is when. おてあらい (washroom) is a place, so you ask どこ.
texts.Add go to the country name to get the la: Add go to the country name to get the language: ちゅうごく becomes ちゅうごくご. English is the odd one out (えいご).
texts.For your own family use the plain words:: For your own family use the plain words: あに, あね, ちち, はは. おにいさん is for someone else's older brother, あね is your own older sister and おとうと is your own younger brother.
texts.kore is for things near the speaker, and: これ is for things near the speaker, and B is the one holding it. それ would be the thing near A, are is far from both, and どれ is the question word.
texts.kata is the polite word for person, and: かた is the polite word for person, and どなた is the polite word for who, so they go together. これ, ここ and どちら mean this, here and which way.
texts.mou ichido onegaishimasu means again, pl: もう いちど おねがいします means again, please. It is what you say in class when you did not catch something.
texts.migi (right) is the opposite of hidari (: みぎ (right) is the opposite of ひだり (left).
texts.Osaka is to the west of Tokyo, so the wo: Osaka is to the west of Tokyo, so the word is にし. ひがし is east, きた is north and みなみ is south.
texts.tanaka san and maria san are people, and: たなか さん and マリア さん are people, and people take います. あります is for things. いません would say that nobody is there, which does not fit since two names were given.
texts.A key and eyeglasses are things, so the: A key and eyeglasses are things, so the verb is あります. People and animals use います.
texts.kissaten and kafe mean the same thing: c: きっさてん and カフェ mean the same thing: coffee shop. デパート is a department store, ほんや is a bookstore and レストラン is a restaurant.
texts.ryou is a dormitory, a place where someo: りょう is a dormitory, a place where someone can be. Do not mix it up with りょうしん, which means parents.
texts.yoko, tonari and soba all mean beside in: よこ, となり and そば all mean beside in the book, so B is agreeing with となり. むこう is across, うしろ is behind and した is under.
texts.aida means between, and it is used with: あいだ means between, and it is used with two things: ぎんこう と カフェ の あいだ。
texts.800 is happyaku. The hundreds 300, 600 a: 800 is はっぴゃく. The hundreds 300, 600 and 800 change their sound: さんびゃく, ろっぴゃく and はっぴゃく。
texts.satsu is the counter for books and noteb: さつ is the counter for books and notebooks. まい is for flat, thin things like paper, ほん is for long things like pencils and こ is for small objects.
texts.ani and watashi make two people, and two: あに and わたし make two people, and two people is ふたり. It is one of the special readings, so learn it as its own word, like ひとり for one person.
texts.Eight years old is hassai. The sound cha: Eight years old is はっさい. The sound changes, so it is not はちさい.
texts.nedan means price. yachin is rent for a: ねだん means price. やちん is rent for a room or house, きっぷ is a ticket and おかね is money in general.
texts.3,000 is sanzen. The special thousands a: 3,000 is さんぜん. The special thousands are 1,000 (せん or いっせん), 3,000 (さんぜん) and 8,000 (はっせん).
texts.(c) juuniman en: (c) じゅうにまん えん
texts.Japanese counts in groups of four digits: Japanese counts in groups of four digits. 120,000 is 12 ten-thousands: じゅうにまん.
texts.zenbu means all or total. The apple and: ぜんぶ means all or total. The apple and the orange together come to 300 yen in all.
texts.If today is Wednesday (suiyoubi), tomorr: If today is Wednesday (すいようび), tomorrow is Thursday, もくようび.
texts.September is kugatsu. Nine is ku in the: September is くがつ. Nine is く in the month names, not きゅう. くげつ would mean nine months.
texts.The 20th has its own reading, hatsuka. I: The 20th has its own reading, はつか. It does not follow the usual にち pattern.
texts.4 o'clock is yoji. The hour four becomes: 4 o'clock is よじ. The hour four becomes よ, so it is not よんじ or しじ。
texts.goro goes with a point in time and means: ごろ goes with a point in time and means around. ぐらい is for amounts, like about 20 minutes. はん would make it 10:30.
texts.kara means from and made means until. go: から means from and まで means until. ごぜん 9-じ から ごご 6-じ まで is from 9 a.m. until 6 p.m.
texts.If this month is October, the next month: If this month is October, the next month is らいげつ. せんげつ is last month, こんげつ is this month and まいつき is every month.
texts.Today is the 10th (tooka), so the 9th (k: Today is the 10th (とおか), so the 9th (ここのか) was yesterday, きのう. おととい is the day before yesterday.
texts.de goes after a vehicle: basu de means b: で goes after a vehicle: バス で means by bus. あるいて already means on foot, so it never takes で. おうふく and かたみち are about tickets.
texts.kan marks how long something lasts. niji: かん marks how long something lasts. にじかん is two hours. にじ would be 2 o'clock, にふん is two minutes and にじゅっぷん is twenty minutes.
texts.mae means before. 2:55 is five minutes b: まえ means before. 2:55 is five minutes before the 3:00 meeting, so 5-fun まえ. すぎ means after.
texts.gurai means about and goes with an amoun: ぐらい means about and goes with an amount of time, here about 15 minutes. ごろ goes with a point in time instead.
texts.katamichi (one way) is already named in: かたみち (one way) is already named in the next sentence, so the first word is おうふく, round trip. It costs more because you travel both ways.
texts.hantoshi is half a year. hitotsuki is on: はんとし is half a year. ひとつき is one month, いちねん is one year and いちじかん is one hour.
texts.zangyou is overtime. The company closes: ざんぎょう is overtime. The company closes at 5 but the work goes on until 8. しゅくだい is homework, アルバイト is a part-time job and かいわ is conversation.
texts.hikouki is an airplane. Manila to Tokyo: ひこうき is an airplane. Manila to Tokyo takes about four hours by plane. A ship would take days, and a bicycle or subway cannot cross the sea.
texts.へやは だいがくの りょうに あります. ryou means dormitor: へやは だいがくの りょうに あります. りょう means dormitory, and the room is in the university dormitory.
texts.つくえの したに かばんが あります. shita means under, s: つくえの したに かばんが あります. した means under, so the bag is under the desk.
texts.つくえの うえに パソコンが あります. ue means on top, so: つくえの うえに パソコンが あります. うえ means on top, so the computer is on the desk.
ごご 7じまで means until 7 p.m. ごご is p.m. and まで means until. The 9 is the opening hour.
texts.ごぜん 8じはんから means from 8:30 a.m. han mean: ごぜん 8じはんから means from 8:30 a.m. はん means half past, so 8じはん is 8:30.
texts.まいしゅう げつようびの ごご 2じ means every Monday at: まいしゅう げつようびの ごご 2じ means every Monday at 2 p.m. まいしゅう is every week, not next week (らいしゅう).
texts.Minami Bookstore. Notebooks are 120 yen: みなみ Bookstore. Notebooks are 120 yen each. Ballpens are 100 yen each. Pencils are 250 yen for five. Open from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. Closed on Sundays.
texts.Chapter 1 teaches you to say what someth: Chapter 1 teaches you to say what something is with the pattern A は B です, and to make it negative or turn it into a question. You learn to answer yes and no, to link nouns with の、と and か, to say "also" with も, to point at things, places and directions, and to ask who, what, where and which. The book writes this chapter in romaji, so this page adds kana to help you start reading.
texts.Chapter 2 teaches you to say where thing: Chapter 2 teaches you to say where things, people and animals are, and whether something exists in a place. You learn the two verbs for being somewhere, あります for things and います for people and animals, and two sentence shapes: A は Location に あります for where something is, and Location に A が あります for what is there. You also learn position words such as うえ, した and なか, and the question words どこ and なに。
texts.Chapter 3 teaches you to count and to ta: Chapter 3 teaches you to count and to talk about amounts. You learn the numbers from 0 up to hundreds of millions, how to ask for and say prices in yen, dollars and pesos, and how to read out a phone number digit by digit. You also learn the counters, which are the short endings you add when you count people, things, animals, ages and floors, such as にん, ほん and ひき. Finally, you learn the question words that ask how many (なん plus the counter) and how counters fit into the sentence shapes you already know.
texts.Chapter 4 teaches you to say when someth: Chapter 4 teaches you to say when something happens. You learn to tell the time, with hours, minutes, a.m. and p.m., and then the days of the week, the months, the days of the month and the years. You also learn the words for yesterday, today, tomorrow, next week and every day. Then you put these time words into sentences: A は time です, from (から), until (まで), exactly (ちょうど) and around (ごろ). Finally, you learn to ask when with いつ and the なん question words, and you meet the four seasons. From this chapter on, the workbook is printed in hiragana.
texts.Chapter 5 teaches you to say how long so: Chapter 5 teaches you to say how long something takes. You move from a point on the clock (4 o'clock) to a length of time (4 hours), and learn the words for minutes, hours, days, weeks, months and years. Then you use them in sentences: A は Span of Time です, how often (に), about (ぐらい), from and up to a place (から, まで), before and after (まえ, すぎ) and by vehicle (で). Finally, you learn the verb かかります for what it takes in time or money, and how to ask with どのぐらい, the なん question words and いくらぐらい。
texts.Chapter 6 teaches you to describe things: Chapter 6 teaches you to describe things with adjectives. There are two types, い-adjectives (たかい) and な-adjectives (きれい), and you learn the 21 basic pairs of opposites. Then you use adjectives in front of a noun (たかい たてもの, きれいな へや), join two adjectives (あかるくて ひろい, きれい で やさしい), and change them for the negative and past (たかくない, たかかった, きれい じゃ ありません, きれいでした). You also learn to ask with どう and どんな, and to say very, a little and not very with とても, たいへん, ちょっと and あまり。
texts.Chapter 7 teaches you your first verbs,: Chapter 7 teaches you your first verbs, so you can talk about your daily routine. You learn the four formal verb endings (ます, ません, ました, ません でした) and the verbs for waking up, sleeping, working, studying and resting. Then you say when things happen with に, から, まで, ごろ and で, describe how an action is done with adverbs made from い-adjectives and な-adjectives (はやく おきます, しずかに べんきょうします), and say how often with いつも, ときどき and ぜんぜん。
texts.Chapter 8 teaches you what you do to thi: Chapter 8 teaches you what you do to things: eat, drink, read, write, buy, sell, sing and call. You learn the new food, drink and reading words and 13 everyday verbs, then the small markers that say who and what and where. O marks the thing you act on, で marks the place, the method or the tool, に marks who receives the action, and と marks who does it with you. You also learn the question words that go with each marker (なにを, どこで, だれ に, だれ と, なにで, どうやって) and some handy phrases from short conversations.
texts.Chapter 9 teaches you how to say where y: Chapter 9 teaches you how to say where you go and where you come from. You learn the motion verbs いきます, きます, かえります and もどります, and the markers that go with them: へ or に for the destination, で for the vehicle, to for the companion, で for the number of people, and に, から, まで and ごろ for time. You also learn the ending words ね and よ, then meet the dictionary form, the casual twin of every ます verb, and the rules for changing from one form to the other.
texts.Chapter 10 teaches you how to speak casu: Chapter 10 teaches you how to speak casually, the way you talk with family and close friends. You learn to build noun + する verbs, and the four informal verb forms: the dictionary form (present positive), the ない form (present negative), the た form (past positive) and the なかった form (past negative). You sort verbs into Groups 1 to 5, Regular verbs and Special verbs, learn how to change between the formal and casual styles, and meet the casual question ending の and the soft ending わ that women often use.
texts.Hiragana and katakana are two ways of wr: Hiragana and katakana are two ways of writing the same 46 sounds. Every hiragana has a katakana twin that says exactly the same thing, so this page teaches them as pairs: each row shows the hiragana and katakana side by side, with tips for both. Learn one sound and you get two shapes. Hiragana is for Japanese words, word endings and small grammar words like は, no and です. Katakana is for words borrowed from other languages, foreign names, sound effects and emphasis.
texts.This lesson covers kanji 31 to 60 of the: This lesson covers kanji 31 to 60 of the JLRC N5 Kanji Workbook. Kanji 31 to 40 are the language of time: half, minutes, hours, weeks and years, plus the words for this, last, next and every. Kanji 41 to 50 are the parts of the day, the four seasons and 正 (correct). Kanji 51 to 60 are positions and directions: up, down, left, right, inside, outside and the four points of the compass. Many example words reuse かんじ from Kanji 1, like 一, 日, 月 and 人.
texts.Chapters 1 to 5 build on each other: fir: Chapters 1 to 5 build on each other: first one basic sentence, then where things are, then how many there are, then when something happens, and then how long it takes. Japanese is shown first in every chapter. Use the reading aids to reveal romaji when you need it; kana readings and English have their own controls.
